In summary, we derive new insights into LM modal categorization using techniques from mechanistic interpretability, with the potential to inform our understanding of modal categorization in humans.

items.title: Majority Bit-Aware Watermarking For Large Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2508.03829v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The growing deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has raised concerns about their misuse in generating harmful or deceptive content. To address this issue, watermarking methods have been proposed to embed identifiable multi-bit messages into generated text for misuse tracing. However, existing methods often suffer from a fundamental trade-off between text quality and decoding accuracy. In particular, they have to restrict the size of the preferred token set (i.e., green list) during encoding to maintain a detectable watermark signal for decoding, which inevitably degrades generation quality. To improve this trade-off, we propose a novel message encoding paradigm called \textit{majority bit-aware encoding}, which relaxes the watermark signal strength from the green list size. This strategy allows for a strong watermark signal to be preserved in generated texts even when using a large green list. We introduce two instantiations of this paradigm: MajorMark and MajorMark$^{+}$, where the latter is specifically optimized for long messages. Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that our methods achieve higher decoding accuracy and superior text quality compared to prior baselines. The code is at https://github.com/JiiahaoXU/MajorMark.

items.title: Scaling Personality Control in LLMs with Big Five Scaler Prompts
items.description: arXiv:2508.06149v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Big5-Scaler, a prompt-based framework for conditioning large language models (LLMs) with controllable Big Five personality traits. By embedding numeric trait values into natural language prompts, our method enables fine-grained personality control without additional training. We evaluate Big5-Scaler across trait expression, dialogue generation, and human trait imitation tasks. Results show that it induces consistent and distinguishable personality traits across models, with performance varying by prompt type and scale. Our analysis highlights the effectiveness of concise prompts and lower trait intensities, providing a efficient approach for building personality-aware dialogue agents.

items.title: Anticipatory Evaluation of Language Models: Predicting LLM Benchmark Scores from Descriptions
items.description: arXiv:2509.20645v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern ML research increasingly faces an evaluation bottleneck: building benchmarks and running experiments is costly, slowing iteration. We ask how much can be inferred about evaluation outcomes before experiments, given only a natural-language description of the task and setup. We call this setting anticipatory evaluation. We introduce EVALCAST, a literature-grounded resource of 2,290 description-performance pairs from 1,519 arXiv papers, including a test set of papers published after the model's knowledge cutoff. We evaluate two tasks: predicting absolute performance through regression and comparing benchmark difficulty through pairwise prediction. Experiments with frontier LLMs show that accurate regression remains challenging, while pairwise predictions can recover relative performance ordering under matched settings. Comparable performance on post-cutoff and streaming evaluations suggests that the observed signal is not solely attributable to previously reported results. Overall, EVALCAST provides a resource and evaluation framework for studying anticipatory evaluation and its potential use in prioritizing benchmarks.

items.title: Eigen-Agent: Adaptive Multi-Agent Scientific Reasoning with Monitor-Based RAG
items.description: arXiv:2509.21193v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong progress on scientific reasoning, yet two major bottlenecks remain. First, explicit retrieval fragments reasoning, imposing a hidden "tool tax" of extra tokens and steps. Second, multi-agent pipelines often dilute strong solutions by averaging across all candidates. We address these challenges with a unified framework that combines implicit retrieval and structured collaboration. At its foundation, a Monitor-based retrieval module operates at the token level, integrating external knowledge with minimal disruption to reasoning. On top of this substrate, Hierarchical Solution Refinement (HSR) iteratively designates each candidate as an anchor to be repaired by its peers, while Quality-Aware Iterative Reasoning (QAIR) adapts refinement to solution quality. On Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) Bio/Chem Gold, our framework achieves 48.3% accuracy - the highest reported to date, surpassing the strongest agent baseline by 13.4 points and leading frontier LLMs by up to 18.1 points, while simultaneously reducing token usage by 53.5% and agent steps by 43.7%. Results on SuperGPQA and TRQA confirm robustness across domains. Error analysis shows that reasoning failures and knowledge gaps co-occur in over 85% of cases, while diversity analysis reveals a clear dichotomy: retrieval tasks benefit from solution variety, whereas reasoning tasks favor consensus. Together, these findings demonstrate how implicit augmentation and structured refinement overcome the inefficiencies of explicit tool use and uniform aggregation. The code is available at https://github.com/tangxiangru/Eigen-1.

items.title: EconCausal: A Context-Aware Economic Reasoning Benchmark for Large Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2510.07231v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Socio-economic causal effects depend heavily on their institutional and environmental contexts. The same intervention can produce different, even opposite, effects across regulatory regimes, market conditions, time periods, or populations. This poses a challenge for large language models (LLMs) in decision-support roles: can they infer the direction of a causal effect under a specified context, and revise that judgment when the context changes? To address this, we introduce EconCausal, a large-scale benchmark of 10,490 context-annotated causal triplets extracted from 2,595 high-quality empirical studies in top-tier economics and finance journals, constructed through a rigorous four-stage pipeline with multi-run consensus, context refinement, and multi-critic filtering. Across 19 models, we observe source-sign over-transfer in cross-context prediction. While top models reach ~84% accuracy in single-context prediction, mean accuracy is 74.75% overall but drops to 44.27% when source and target signs disagree. On these cases, accuracy is 11.54 percentage points (pp) lower with the signed source example than with the target input alone. Mean accuracy is below 60% under corrupted source signs. Models also struggle to predict study-reported nonsignificant effects (19.16% accuracy). The dataset and benchmark are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/econcausal-benchmark-6F12.

items.title: LLMs Can Get "Brain Rot": A Pilot Study on Twitter/X
items.description: arXiv:2510.13928v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose and test the LLM Brain Rot Hypothesis: continual exposure to junk web text induces lasting cognitive decline in large language models (LLMs). To unveil junk effects, we designed a novel controlled experiment on real Twitter/X corpora, by constructing junk and reverse-controlled datasets via two orthogonal operationalizations: M1 (engagement degree) and M2 (semantic quality), with matched token scale and training operations across conditions. Compared to the control group, continual pre-training of 4 LLMs on the junk dataset causes non-trivial declines (Hedges' g>0.3) on reasoning, long-context understanding, safety, and inflating "dark traits" (e.g., psychopathy, narcissism). The gradual mixtures of junk and control datasets also yield dose-response cognition decay: for example, under M1, ARC-Challenge with Chain-of-Thought drops 72.1 -> 57.2 and RULER-CWE 83.7 -> 52.3 as junk ratio rises from 0% to 100%. Error forensics reveal several key insights. First, we identify thought-skipping as the primary lesion in reasoning: models increasingly truncate or skip chains. Second, partial but incomplete healing is observed: scaling instruction tuning and clean continual pre-training improve the declined cognition, yet cannot restore baseline capability, suggesting persistent representational drift rather than format mismatch. Finally, we discover that the popularity, a non-semantic metric, of a tweet is a better indicator of the Brain Rot effect than the length in M1. Together, the results provide significant, multi-perspective evidence that social effects of data could be a causal driver of LLM capability decay in continual pre-training, thereby motivating routine "cognitive health checks" for deployed and evolving LLMs.

items.title: Reclaiming Low-Quality Instruction Data with Rule-Guided LLM Reconstruction
items.description: arXiv:2510.23160v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Data selection for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) often discards low-scoring instruction examples that may retain useful supervision. We propose a rule-guided LLM reconstruction framework to reclaim this information. The framework identifies low-scoring samples through LLM-based rating and score correction, selects semantically representative sources, and reconstructs instruction-response pairs through strategy-guided generation, criteria-based validation, and failure-guided repair. From 123,786 low-scoring samples, it constructs 54,888 training examples. Across three 7B/8B base LLMs, the reconstructed data achieves higher average downstream performance than the low-scoring source set and all evaluated data-selection baselines. Despite using substantially fewer examples than the full source dataset (approximately 300K), it achieves higher reported average scores than full-data training across all three base models. Stepwise ablations identify rule-guided reconstruction as the largest source of observed improvements over direct fusion, while a manual audit reveals remaining limitations in source integration and answer faithfulness. These findings support reconstruction as a complementary approach to selection-based SFT data curation.

items.title: QuantEval: A Benchmark for Financial Quantitative Tasks in Large Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2601.08689v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in finance-oriented question answering, yet their evaluation on professional quantitative workflows remains fragmented and often stops at factual or document-grounded QA. We introduce QuantEval, a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can complete the compute--implement--validate loop required in quantitative finance. QuantEval contains 1,575 expert-validated instances across three complementary dimensions: (i) knowledge-based QA, (ii) quantitative mathematical reasoning, and (iii) quantitative strategy coding. The coding task is evaluated with a deterministic CTA-style backtesting framework that executes model-generated strategies and compares risk--return metrics against expert references, moving beyond syntax or template matching. We evaluate 13 open-source and proprietary LLMs, report prompt and reliability analyses, and observe substantial gaps relative to human experts, especially in multi-step reasoning and framework-constrained coding. We further conduct supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning experiments on domain-aligned data, showing that training can improve quantitative reasoning while also exposing trade-offs in factual recall. QuantEval releases the dataset, evaluation scripts, and full backtesting configuration to support reproducible research on LLMs for quantitative finance.

items.title: CALM-IT: Enhancing Synthetic Motivational Interviewing Dialogue Quality with Conversational Dynamics
items.description: arXiv:2601.10085v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conversational dynamics describe how rapport, emotion, and goals change over a dialogue. These changes are important in therapeutic conversations, where they can influence when and how therapists intervene. However, large language model (LLM)-based synthetic therapeutic dialogue generators rarely track how these properties evolve together, which may limit the quality of longer conversations. We introduce CALM-IT, a dual-agent framework that tracks client states and therapist-side inferences to guide strategy selection and utterance generation. We evaluate synthetic Motivational Interviewing (MI) dialogues using automated Motivational Interviewing Treatment Integrity (MITI) ratings, conversational metrics, and comparisons across dialogue lengths, with ratings from four licensed psychologists providing support for key findings. Across 8,232 dialogues covering 686 grounded scenarios, four frameworks, and three target lengths, CALM-IT achieves the highest mean scores on all four MITI 4.2 global ratings and shows the smallest aggregate change in quality between short- and long-form conditions. CALM-IT also achieves the highest simulated client redirection acceptance rate (64.3\%), with its strongest redirections followed by increased change talk and reduced sustain talk. Ablation experiments show that removing conversational dynamics components reduces dialogue quality. Together, these results suggest that explicitly modeling conversational dynamics can improve the quality and consistency of long-form synthetic MI dialogues.

items.title: MasalBench: A Benchmark for Contextual and Cross-Cultural Understanding of Persian Proverbs in LLMs
items.description: arXiv:2601.22050v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In recent years, multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) have become an inseparable part of daily life, making it crucial for them to master the rules of conversational language in order to communicate effectively with users. While previous work has evaluated LLMs' understanding of figurative language in high-resource languages, their performance in low-resource languages remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce MasalBench, a comprehensive benchmark for assessing LLMs' contextual and cross-cultural understanding of Persian proverbs, which are a key component of conversation in this low-resource language. We evaluate eight state-of-the-art LLMs on MasalBench and find that they perform well in identifying Persian proverbs in context, achieving accuracies above 0.90. However, their performance drops considerably when tasked with identifying equivalent English proverbs, with the best model achieving 0.79 accuracy. Our findings highlight the limitations of current LLMs in cultural knowledge and analogical reasoning, and they provide a framework for assessing cross-cultural understanding in other low-resource languages. MasalBench is available at https://github.com/kalhorghazal/MasalBench.

items.title: Language Steering for Multilingual In-Context Learning
items.description: arXiv:2602.02326v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: If multilingual language model representations contain separable language-associated structure, then shifting between languages may require only simple activation-space interventions. To test this hypothesis, we study multilingual in-context learning (ICL) as a controlled setting: few-shot demonstrations are provided in English while the test query is in a target language, creating a clear cross-lingual transfer challenge. We propose language vectors, which are computed as mean activation differences between parallel source and target language examples at a particular layer and applied as inference-time offsets to the model's hidden states. Across three tasks spanning 19 languages and three models, our method improves over English few-shot prompting without any parameter updates. Beyond performance, the vectors encode interpretable linguistic structure: closely related languages form tight clusters, and vectors transfer effectively across tasks and languages, with closely related languages' vectors recovering more of the gain than distant ones. Together, these findings suggest that language occupies structured directions in multilingual activation space, and that inference-time interventions on English demonstrations can narrow the cross-lingual ICL gap.

items.title: Geometric Alignment without Functional Equivalence: A Layer-wise Analysis of the Speech-Text Modality Gap
items.description: arXiv:2603.01502v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: End-to-end speech large language models (LLMs) often answer the same question less accurately from speech than from text, even when the spoken content matches the text prompt. Existing analyses study this modality gap through the geometry of representations and measure how closely speech representations align with text. Geometric alignment gives the gap a measurable form, but it does not show whether the model uses aligned representations in the same way. This work connects representation geometry with answer formation and asks whether geometric alignment implies functional equivalence. We compare cross-layer Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) with layer-wise answer margins for four open-weight speech LLMs on SpeechMMLU and VoiceBench BBH. In Qwen2.5-Omni and MiniCPM-o, speech and text representations align in middle layers while their late-layer answer margins still differ, so mid-layer alignment does not imply functional equivalence. Qwen2-Audio instead shows weak alignment, which indicates a different failure mode. An attention intervention at fixed input and token count identifies a causal effect of late attention allocation on answer-code separation, a quantity distinct from answer correctness. Compressing the speech signal or its token sequence repairs a subset of the errors that occur only with speech.

items.title: LoopRPT: Reinforcement Pre-Training for Looped Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2603.19714v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Looped language models (LoopLMs) perform iterative latent computation to refine internal representations, offering an alternative to explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. However, existing reinforcement learning (RL) paradigms primarily target output tokens, creating a structural mismatch with looped architectures whose reasoning unfolds implicitly. In this work, we propose LoopRPT, a reinforcement pre-training framework tailored for LoopLMs. By reframing next-token prediction as a next-token reasoning task, LoopRPT assigns reinforcement signals directly to latent steps using an EMA teacher reference and noisy latent rollouts. This formulation enables RL to directly shape intermediate representations, compressing effective reasoning into fewer iterations. We instantiate LoopRPT on Ouro across multiple model scales. Results show that LoopRPT improves per-step representation quality and achieves Pareto dominance in accuracy-computation trade-offs. Large gains on hard tokens indicate that LoopRPT enhances early-stage reasoning rather than merely encouraging premature exits. Our findings highlight reinforcement pre-training as a principled paradigm for learning efficient latent reasoning in LoopLMs.

items.title: PLACID: Privacy-preserving Large language models for Acronym Clinical Inference and Disambiguation
items.description: arXiv:2603.23678v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer transformative solutions across many domains, but healthcare integration is hindered by strict data privacy constraints. Clinical narratives are dense with ambiguous acronyms, misinterpretation these abbreviations can precipitate severe outcomes like life-threatening medication errors. While cloud-dependent LLMs excel at Acronym Disambiguation, transmitting Protected Health Information to external servers violates privacy frameworks. To bridge this gap, this study pioneers the evaluation of small-parameter models deployed entirely on-device to ensure privacy preservation. We introduce a privacy-preserving cascaded pipeline leveraging general-purpose local models to detect clinical acronyms, routing them to domain-specific biomedical models for context-relevant expansions. Results reveal that while general instruction-following models achieve high detection accuracy (~0.988), their expansion capabilities plummet (~0.655). Our cascaded approach utilizes domain-specific medical models to increase expansion accuracy to (~0.81). This novel work demonstrates that privacy-preserving, on-device (2B-10B) models deliver high-fidelity clinical acronym disambiguation support.

items.title: AdaptFuse: Training-Free Sequential Preference Inference via Externalized Bayesian Computation
items.description: arXiv:2604.03925v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle to accumulate evidence across multiple rounds of user interactions, failing to update their beliefs in a manner consistent with Bayesian inference. Existing solutions require fine-tuning on sensitive user interaction data, limiting their applicability in privacy-conscious settings. We propose \textsc{AdaptFuse}, a training-free framework that externalizes probabilistic computation entirely from the LLM, where a symbolic module maintains a Bayesian posterior over a discrete hypothesis set, while a frozen LLM contributes semantic reasoning via multi-sample Dirichlet aggregation. The two signals are combined through entropy-adaptive fusion, which automatically weights each source by its predictive confidence, shifting reliance from the LLM to the symbolic posterior as evidence accumulates. We evaluate across three domains: flight recommendation, hotel recommendation, and web shopping; on Gemma~2 9B, Llama~3 8B, and Qwen~2.5 7B. \textsc{AdaptFuse} consistently outperforms both prompting baselines and fine-tuned Bayesian Teaching models on all tasks, with accuracy improving monotonically over interaction rounds. These results demonstrate that principled inference-time algorithms can substitute for fine-tuning in personalized recommendation, without storing or training on sensitive user data.

items.title: Phantom Paradoxes: Language Models Treat Unresolved Circular Truth Dependence as Contradiction
items.description: arXiv:2604.12128v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Do language models struggle with self-reference itself, or with structures where propagating truth values along references cannot settle a value in finitely many steps? Our results support the latter. In our main test, statements refer to one another's truth in a cycle, yet exactly one consistent assignment exists. Local propagation never settles the queried value, but exhaustive search finds it, so INCONSISTENT (no consistent assignment) is always wrong. We call such misreadings of satisfiable problems phantom paradoxes. Each circular problem has a grounded twin with the same answer but no cycle. To rule out logical difficulty and unfamiliar wording, we added constraint twins (equivalent formulas without talk of truth) and perplexity-matched grounded controls. In confirmatory behavioral tests fixed before any confirmation response, four open models from three families answered INCONSISTENT on average 31.0 percentage points more often on circular problems than on grounded twins, 36.4 more than on constraint twins and 37.1 more than on perplexity-matched controls. In each model, validated layer-wise truth directions, fitted on unrelated arithmetic, recovered the queried value at the question's last token for grounded twins but not for circular problems. Constraint twins, likewise unrecovered, drew INCONSISTENT far less often, so circular truth dependence, not the unrecovered value alone, matters. In a small natural-language bank, self-reference settling in finitely many steps drew INCONSISTENT 23.4 points less often than unsettled self-reference with the same classical solution. Pooled tests did not show the predicted late-layer revision or attention spread. Overall, models treat unresolved circular truth dependence as contradiction. We will release all prompts, outputs and hidden states.

items.title: Latent Preference Modeling for Multi-Session Personalized Tool Calling
items.description: arXiv:2604.17886v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Users often omit essential details in their requests to LLM-based agents, resulting in under-specified inputs for tool use. This poses a fundamental challenge for tool-augmented agents, as API execution typically requires complete arguments, highlighting the need for personalized tool calling. To study this problem, we present Multi-Session Personalized Tool Calling (MPT), a benchmark comprising 4,695 instances over 459 multi-session interaction histories that cover three challenges: Preference Recall, Induction, and Transfer. We further propose PRefine, a test-time memory method that maintains the user's latent preference as a textual hypothesis revised through a generate--verify--refine loop. Across five LLMs, existing memory systems often fail to improve on full-history prompting; PRefine outperforms all baselines and alone surpasses it on Preference Transfer. These results indicate that memory for personalized agents must abstract behavior into preferences, rather than simply archive it.

items.title: ContextWeaver: Selective and Dependency-Structured Memory Construction for LLM Agents
items.description: arXiv:2604.23069v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents often struggle in long-context interactions. As the history grows, sliding windows and prompt compression may drop earlier information that later steps rely on. Retrieval-based memory systems surface relevant content but still overlook the causal and logical dependencies between steps. We introduce ContextWeaver, a selective and dependency-structured memory framework that organizes an agent's interaction trace into a graph of reasoning steps and selects the relevant context for future actions. ContextWeaver supports (1) dependency-based construction and traversal that link each step to the earlier steps it relies on; (2) compact dependency summaries of the reasoning paths; and (3) a lightweight validation layer that incorporates execution feedback. On five software-engineering and terminal benchmarks with a fixed budget per task, ContextWeaver improves the resolve rate over a sliding-window baseline on all five, with a significant gain when pooled across benchmarks, while using 13-18% fewer agent steps. It also performs favorably against alternative context-management approaches, with the largest gains on long-horizon repository tasks. On SWE-Bench Pro, ContextWeaver raises the resolve rate from 66.5% to 72.6%, with significant improvements across all three model backbones. The improvement also holds when the sliding window's budget is raised to cover the summary cost.

items.title: On Challenges in Evaluation Methodology: A Review
items.description: arXiv:2604.25923v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advances in language models have prompted a growing body of work that questions prevailing evaluation practices. However, many such critiques have already been discussed in natural language processing (NLP), a field with a long history of methodological reflection on evaluation. We conduct a scoping review spanning four decades and develop a taxonomy of 22 recurring concerns. For each concern, we examine how recently it was discussed in the reviewed literature and whether it receives explicit attention in institutional checklists, finding that some concerns have become less visible in literature and many lack coverage in these checklists. Our work provides an overview of the major concerns in evaluation methodology that have shaped the field and identifies potential targets for renewed investigation and field-level intervention by the research community.

items.title: When Can Digital Personas Reliably Approximate Human Survey Findings?
items.description: arXiv:2605.10659v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Digital personas powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as substitutes for human survey respondents, yet it remains unclear when they can reliably approximate human survey findings. We answer this question using the LISS panel, constructing personas from respondents' background variables and pre-2023 survey histories, then testing them against the same respondents' held-out post-cutoff answers. Across four persona architectures, three LLMs, and two prediction tasks, we assess performance at the question, respondent, distributional, equity, and clustering levels. Digital personas improve alignment with human response distributions, especially in domains tied to stable attributes and values, but remain limited for individual prediction and fail to recover multivariate respondent structure. Retrieval-augmented architectures provide the clearest gains, but performance depends more on human response structure than on model choice: personas perform best for low-variability questions and common respondent patterns, and worst for subjective, heterogeneous, or rare responses. Our results provide practical guidance on when digital personas could be appropriate for survey research and when human validation remains necessary.

items.title: When Reasoning Supervision Hurts: TTCW-Based Long-Form Literary Review Generation
items.description: arXiv:2605.20364v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automatic evaluation of long-form literary writing remains challenging, particularly for creativity-related dimensions such as originality and flexibility. We address the lack of large-scale supervision for structured Torrance Test of Creative Writing (TTCW)-based evaluation by constructing a dataset of 263{,}911 long-form stories, each paired with scalar scores and meta-synthesised review comments across 14 TTCW-based dimensions. Using this dataset, we study whether reviewer-style reasoning traces improve structured literary review generation across Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Nemotron-8B. Across all three models, no-trace supervision yields higher score imitation fidelity and near-complete report generation, whereas trace supervision reduces completion to $85.9$--$90.9\%$. Failure analysis shows that $88.6\%$ of failed reasoning generations contain semantic repetition loops inside the trace. These loops concentrate in particular story--criterion interactions and progressively harden after onset, while comparable repetition is rare in the supervision data. Our results suggest that, for long-form tasks requiring strictly structured outputs, explicit reasoning traces can introduce generation instability that outweighs their overall benefit.

items.title: ConRAG: Consensus-Driven Evidence Flow for Multi-Hop Question Answering
items.description: arXiv:2605.28093v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing large language models (LLMs) on multi-hop question answering (QA), which requires reasoning over evidence from multiple documents. However, current multi-hop RAG approaches still struggle with evidence selection and information transfer, i.e., retrieving irrelevant passages or failing to pass intermediate information to subsequent reasoning steps, thereby hindering coherent multi-hop reasoning. To this end, we propose ConRAG, a consensus-driven evidence flow framework that effectively boosts LLM performance on complex multi-hop QA. In short, the core of ConRAG is to select relevant evidence via consensus-driven multi-view ranking, and leverage a slot-based mechanism to transfer intermediate information between dependent reasoning steps. Extensive experiments across three multi-hop QA benchmarks show that ConRAG surpasses the baselines by a clear margin. Encouragingly, on Gemma-4-31B-it, ConRAG outperforms the strongest baseline by 5.8 points in average score, while reducing total end-to-end runtime and token consumption by 75.9% and 67.3%, respectively.

items.title: Robust Asynchronous Planning via Auto-Formalization
items.description: arXiv:2606.00981v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLMs can plan by generating schedules directly as a Planner, or by translating a task into a formal specification for a solver as a Formalizer. Most real-world tasks are asynchronous, with non-uniform durations, concurrency, and execution-time changes, yet existing benchmarks hardly cover them. We unify asynchronous planning under one formulation and release three benchmarks spanning task-graph scale, grounded state and resource constraints, and execution-time events. Surprisingly, PDDL2.1, the formalism built for temporal planning, is the weakest pipeline. On AsyncPlan-XXL it averages 30.8% plan accuracy, against 81.7% for the Planner and 94.0% for a CP-SAT Formalizer. The gap widens with scale, and at 100 actions the three pipelines reach 9.0%, 44.5%, and 82.5%, respectively. The formalism is not to blame. Compiled from the same model-extracted intermediate representation, PDDL2.1 and CP-SAT reach nearly identical accuracy (81.6% vs. 81.5%), and gold task graphs reach 100% for both. What remains is a bottleneck shared by every pipeline: recovering the task graph from language. Execution-time events further degrade every pipeline, yet updating only event-induced constraints reaches 81.6% versus 41.6% for full regeneration. Robust asynchronous planning thus hinges not on the expressiveness of the target formalism but on how reliably a model can write and edit it, and a well-chosen interface can let a weaker model match a stronger one.

items.title: Ouvia: A User-centered Framework for Measuring Usability of Speech Translation in Real-World Communication Scenarios
items.description: arXiv:2606.06177v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speech translation (ST) is increasingly adopted in user applications, yet its evaluation largely focuses on decontextualized testbeds and holistic quality, rather than end users' communication needs. We introduce Ouvia, an evaluation framework for measuring user-perceived usability of speech translation outputs in real-world settings. Ouvia focuses on one-to-one communication: an English speaker needs to convey a request to a Portuguese speaker, and the message is automatically translated. Through a custom web app and multi-phase study design, we collect more than 1,750 such interactions in healthcare and everyday situations, mediated by four ST systems, involving speakers from three English dialects and two genders. We find that modern ST serves people only to a limited extent---only around half of interactions are rated as usable---with significant gaps in reported usability across demographic groups. Moreover, among quality metrics, we find that QA-based evaluation is a substantially stronger predictor of real-world usability than standard approaches. Together, these findings stress the importance of situated, user-centered evaluation frameworks that go beyond holistic quality scores and attend to who the technology serves---and how well.

items.title: Explain Like I'm 5 or Whatever I Choose: Evaluating the Potential for Interactive Complexity in Language Model Responses
items.description: arXiv:2606.06788v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Given the increased use of large language models (LLMs) for reading and seeking information and the varying needs and backgrounds of users, direct manipulation of text can be a valuable mechanism for end-user control. However, enabling direct manipulation requires that models generate text consistent with user-requested changes. We focus on one such setting, manipulating the complexity of scientific information, and ask if models can generate multiple summaries along a continuum of text complexity that enable effective user selection and control. Through a within-subjects user study, we identify reliable complexity measures and a criterion for how models should conform to these measures. We evaluate five LLMs of different families, sizes, and reasoning abilities on $557$ scientific queries. We find that while models can vary complexity across responses, most changes remain inconsistent, with models shifting the complexity measures in the correct direction at most $33.67$% of the time.

items.title: When More Documents Hurt RAG: Measuring and Reducing Vector Search Dilution with Domain-Scoped Retrieval
items.description: arXiv:2606.11350v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) degrades when applied to large, heterogeneous document collections. In RAG systems, dense similarity becomes less discriminative, causing top-$k$ retrieval to return semantically similar but contextually incorrect chunks. We refer to this failure mode as vector search dilution. Even under hybrid dense+sparse retrieval, we first observed it in a deployed Wyoming Department of Transportation (WYDOT) system; in a controlled experiment, growing the corpus from 54 to 1,128 documents cut precision@10 by 63% and recall of the answer-bearing document by 23%. Similar patterns were observed in six other DOTs. To diagnose this issue, we introduce MASDR-RAG (Metadata-Scoped Domain Retrieval for RAG) as a controlled testbed over 200 human-validated queries, five LLM backbones, six public benchmark corpora, and two index stacks. In MASDR-RAG, domain scoping is the load-bearing component. We found hard partitioning to be unsafe, whereas training-free soft scoping is safe when the scope structure is real. Furthermore, we can discover these scopes without hand-curated metadata. However, multi-agent orchestration triggers a precision-faithfulness paradox that survives format controls, prompt controls, and blind human evaluation. Based on these varied outcomes, our practical recommendation is simple: soft-scope first, then perform a single synthesis call.

items.title: ProReviewer: Evidence-Driven Investigation for Scientific Peer Review
items.description: arXiv:2606.13349v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Effective peer review requires adaptive investigation that responds to evidence emerging from each paper. Existing LLM-based reviewers largely organize the review process around predefined workflows, leaving limited scope for emerging evidence to reshape investigation. We propose ProReviewer, an evidence-driven review agent that formulates reviewing as a Markov Decision Process, with a structured review log forming the core of its state. At each step, the agent uses accumulated findings to decide what to inspect next and when to conclude. As new evidence emerges, it updates the log by revising claim statuses, resolving open questions, and recording new findings. Each point in the final review cites supporting log entries, making its judgments traceable to the recorded evidence. On 1,000 held-out ICLR 2026 papers, the trained 8B ProReviewer achieves the highest average score among all compared methods, including those built on a 397B model; human evaluators prefer its reviews over all baselines on three of four review-quality dimensions.

items.title: HiMPO: Hindsight-Informed Memory Policy Optimization for Less-Entangled Credit in Long-Horizon Agents
items.description: arXiv:2606.16285v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-horizon agents compress interaction histories into memory, but final outcomes entangle memory-writing credit with tool failures and reasoning errors. We propose HiMPO, a Hindsight-Informed Memory Policy Optimization framework that supplements trajectory-level reinforcement learning with memory-specific credit. For each update, HiMPO compares the target answer's log-likelihood under the previous and updated memories while holding the remaining pre-write context fixed. A soft gate based on group-relative hindsight relevance then weights the local utility advantage. Trajectory-level credit applies to all generated tokens; memory tokens additionally receive the auxiliary advantage. Across judge-based open-domain tasks and objective compressive-memory QA, HiMPO improves task performance while preserving compressed-context efficiency. On Local Wiki Search, it improves average F1 and exact match over MemPO by 2.6 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Controlled interventions and live memory-reversion studies provide evidence of reduced blame leakage and alignment between memory credit and behavioral effects. With the policy fixed, the credit estimator remains robust to the tested forms of target noise.

items.title: DEEPRUBRIC: Evidence-Tree Rubric Supervision for Efficient Reinforcement Learning of Deep Research Agents
items.description: arXiv:2606.17029v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep research agents synthesize long-form reports by searching and reasoning over retrieved evidence. Reinforcement learning with rubric-based rewards improves these agents by optimizing them against checkable criteria that translate report quality into reward signals, but its efficiency depends on whether those criteria reliably capture the task scope and evidence needs. Most existing studies ask an LLM to generate rubrics for a given query, but when the model fails to infer the underlying information needs, the generated rubrics may be incomplete and reduce RL efficiency. To obtain more reliable query--rubric supervision, we introduce DeepRubric, a data construction framework that reverses this process: instead of inferring evaluation criteria for a given query, it first determines what an evidence-backed report should be evaluated on and then synthesizes aligned query--rubric pairs from those evaluation targets. Starting from a sampled seed topic, DeepRubric builds an evidence tree by recursively expanding evidence-backed sub-questions, whose leaves serve as atomic and verifiable evaluation targets. It then uses the evidence tree to synthesize the training query and rubrics, ensuring that the reward evaluates exactly the information requested by the query. Using DeepRubric, we construct 9K query--rubric supervision examples and train DeepRubric-8B with rubric-based GRPO, achieving comparable performance to prior open state-of-the-art deep research models across three benchmarks with roughly 13x fewer RL GPU-hours.

items.title: Confidently Wrong: Detecting Hallucinations in Financial Question Answering from LLM Internal States
items.description: arXiv:2607.11414v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in financial applications fail most consequentially when they are confidently wrong. Hedged, uncertain answers invite scrutiny, whereas confident errors silently degrade downstream decisions without warning. We ask how reliably such confidently wrong answers, or confident hallucinations, can be detected from a model's internal activations, and whether those activations carry information beyond its output-level confidence signals. We train linear probes on the residual stream and evaluate them on two established numerical question-answering (QA) benchmarks built from real filings, FinQA and TAT-QA. Behavioral confidence is measured as the agreement among eight resampled answers to the same question, and probe effectiveness is compared against baselines, such as token log-probabilities and the model's own True/False self-assessment of its answer. Our findings show that among confident answers, those for which all eight resamples agree, 15-23% are wrong on FinQA. There the probes have a significant advantage over output-level baselines in detecting hallucinations, holding 0.68-0.77 AUROC while the best baselines fall to 0.55-0.63, across Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Gemma-2-9B. Our results suggest that probing can be a cost-effective triage mechanism for routing LLM answers to human review and quality control procedures in high-stakes financial applications. Code and data are available at https://github.com/richardzhewang/confidently-wrong.

items.title: Every Time I Hire a Linguist, Inference Costs Go Down: On Linguistic Rules as Effective Prompt Compressors
items.description: arXiv:2607.25335v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Prompt compression shortens LLM input to reduce inference cost, yet existing methods score token importance through LM forward passes. It remains questionable whether such nuanced, costly token selection is necessary. Compression requires identifying informative content, a problem that linguistic research has long addressed through cues that can be operationalized as deterministic rules. We therefore ask: can \textbf{linguistic rules alone} serve as effective prompt compressors, without LM-based scoring at compression time? To address this, we conduct offline evolutionary search over lexical, syntactic, semantic, and discourse seeds to find competitive rule combinations. The resulting linguistic compressor requires no LM forward pass at deployment and uses only CPU-side processing for compression. We evaluate it with a dual-path protocol to balance compression quality and reconstruction fidelity. Across short passages, multi-document reasoning, and dialogue-memory QA datasets, evolved compressors achieve performance similar to that of recent advanced prompt-compression strategies. Performance is strongest under light-to-moderate compression and degrades as compression becomes more aggressive, while the Direct and Reconstruction paths exhibit distinct patterns. Evolutionary analysis reveals that effective compression fuses signals across linguistic levels and, as the compression ratio increases, rules shift from token pruning to sentence extraction.

items.title: Commit Locally, Exit Globally: Coordinating Adaptive Sampling and Early Exit in Diffusion Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2607.28166v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion language models predict tokens in parallel but still require many iterative forward passes. Adaptive sampling accelerates local token commitment, while recent global stopping methods seek to end generation early. Our trajectory analysis shows that short answers can stabilize early in decoding, whereas reasoning outputs often require more steps to settle. A fixed progress threshold therefore struggles to avoid both redundant computation on short-answer tasks and premature termination on reasoning tasks. We introduce C$^4$, a training-free framework that combines local decoding acceleration with adaptive global early exit. Confidence-Verified Early Exit (CVEE) determines when to end generation, skipping the remaining steps once its stopping criterion is met. It combines confidence and temporal agreement to adapt stopping to the observed revision history. Commit-Core-Then-Confirm (CCTC) accelerates token commitment while generation continues, reducing the decoding steps needed to complete each block. It extends confidence-threshold parallel decoding with a boundary-anchored core and one-step confirmation of deferred predictions, constraining additional commitments to mitigate premature freezing under unresolved context. With CVEE calibrated once on LLaDA, the same numerical settings transfer across all 12 zero-shot tasks and to Dream without recalibration. Under this configuration, C$^4$ reduces decoding steps by 64-95% and achieves measured decoding-loop speedups of 2.6x-18.6x, with task performance close to full decoding. Component analyses show complementary contributions: early exit supplies most savings on short-answer tasks, while local acceleration contributes more on reasoning and code generation.

items.title: IACM-RL: Intent-Aware Context Management and Reinforcement Learning for Complex Tool Invocation under Dynamic Intent Fluctuations
items.description: arXiv:2608.02110v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Executing long-horizon tool invocations in real-world environments is severely challenged by dynamic user intent noise. Existing methods attempt robustness via implicit history scanning or text compression, yet predominantly assume perfect instructions in simplistic scenarios. Inevitably, under fluctuating contexts, obsolete constraints dilute model attention, triggering intent deviation and repetitive API loops. To resolve this, we propose IACM-RL, a comprehensive framework for robust tool invocation. First, we introduce the DynamicIntent pipeline, synthesizing trajectories across several fine-grained fluctuation scenarios, paired with a five-dimensional diagnostic metric suite. Second, IACM-RL deploys a BeliefState-based Self-Generated Context Manager that proactively tracks shifting goals and isolates overwritten parameters using structural stale flags. To autonomously internalize this state-tracking capability, we optimize the policy using a hierarchical intent-driven reward alongside two auxiliary losses (CM extraction and state distillation). Experiments on DynamicIntent, BFCL-V3, and $\mathrm{\tau}^2$-Bench demonstrate that IACM-RL outperforms baselines, reducing infinite loops and stale context errors while enhancing out-of-domain generalization.

items.title: ANCHOR-RE: An Agentic Biomedical Relation Extraction Framework with Retrieval Augmentation and Error-Driven Verification
items.description: arXiv:2608.03154v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Biomedical relation extraction (BioRE) supports knowledge graph construction and hypothesis generation. In real-world settings, most candidate entity pairs are unrelated. Symbolic systems such as SemRep offer high precision and interpretability but limited recall, whereas large language models (LLMs) can produce false-positive relations. We developed ANCHOR-RE, an agentic framework that combines retrieved demonstrations, ontology-guided semantic constraints, external biomedical knowledge, and error-driven verification to improve BioRE reliability without task-specific fine-tuning. We evaluated ANCHOR-RE on SemRepGS, DDI, and ChemProt using proprietary and open-weight LLMs. To assess generalizability while reducing potential pretraining contamination, we also conducted a post-cutoff temporal precision evaluation using 100 biomedical articles published in 2026. With the proprietary backbone, ANCHOR-RE improved micro-F1 over direct prompting from 0.654 to 0.676 on SemRepGS, from 0.769 to 0.881 on DDI, and from 0.937 to 0.941 on ChemProt, outperforming previously reported inference-only methods on DDI and ChemProt. Gains were also observed with the open-weight backbone. Additional experiments demonstrated cross-family model compatibility and sensitivity to external knowledge quality. Manual assessment of 500 randomly sampled positive predictions from the post-cutoff set yielded 69% precision. These results show that contextual evidence and error-driven verification can improve BioRE reliability across benchmarks, model families, and newly published literature, supporting ANCHOR-RE as a practical training-free approach to biomedical literature mining.

items.title: Off-the-Shelf Language-Vision Encoders Predict Human Gaze Preferences in Visual World Experiments
items.description: arXiv:2608.07282v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A central question for computational psycholinguistics is to what extent neural language models can serve as cognitively adequate models of human language processing. However, work has been overwhelmingly focused on the unimodal case of written or spoken language. In contrast, multimodal paradigms, like visual world experiments that present participants with both visual and linguistic input simultaneously, have been neglected. In this paper, we present a novel approach that predicts patterns of gaze preferences in visual world studies. To do so, it derives target preferences by applying an attribution method to a simple bi-modal CLIP bi-encoder. We demonstrate the ability of this approach to qualitatively replicate the gaze patterns found in a seminal English visual world study demonstrating human predictive processing. It does so without a generative architecture and without the need for fine-tuning, despite not being trained for the task.

items.title: PERCEPT: A Corpus for POS Tagging and Analysis of Persian-English Code-Mixing
items.description: arXiv:2608.10109v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Social media has become a major venue for multilingual communication, where users frequently mix multiple languages within a single utterance. Although code-mixed corpora have been developed for several language pairs, Persian-English code-mixing remains relatively underexplored. Existing Persian resources lack Universal Dependencies (UD) part-of-speech (POS) annotations for code-mixed words, limiting both linguistic analyses and the development of syntax-aware NLP models. To address this gap, we introduce PERCEPT, the first publicly available large-scale Persian-English code-mixed corpus annotated with Universal Dependencies POS tags for code-mixed words. The dataset comprises 6,800 posts collected from Twitter (X), Instagram, and Digikala, each containing at least one identified Persian-English code-mixed word. We further present an LLM-assisted annotation framework that automatically assigns POS tags and document-level topics. Human evaluation demonstrates high agreement between the automatically generated annotations and gold annotations, confirming the reliability of the annotations. Using PERCEPT, we conduct the first comprehensive linguistic analysis of Persian-English code-mixing across multiple social media platforms. Our analyses reveal that nouns are the predominant category for code-mixed words, while the distributions of other POS categories vary across platforms. We further find that the positional distribution of code-mixed words is remarkably consistent across platforms, whereas the triggering effect is substantially more pronounced in Digikala. PERCEPT is publicly available at https://github.com/kalhorghazal/PERCEPT.

items.title: Hybrid Gated Attention
items.description: arXiv:2608.11805v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gated attention is an effective approach to mitigate attention sinks and enhance the representational capacity of attention. To further extend its effectiveness-efficiency Pareto frontier, we propose a Hybrid Gated Attention (HyGA) framework that contains three types of gating strategies. Specifically, these gates leverage diverse information from multiple stages of attention, and collaboratively build element-wise/head-wise gating from multiple perspectives, capturing intra-head and cross-head information interactions. Through our hybrid gating components, HyGA could provide multi-source modulation signals, enabling more comprehensive control over information flow and improving the representational capacity of attention. We also introduce low-rank matrix decomposition and learnable attention sink to further enhance training efficiency and stability. In experiments, we evaluate HyGA on widely-used benchmarks based on different backbones. The experimental results show that our HyGA comprehensively improves both training loss and various downstream performances compared with Gated attention. HyGA has also been verified to achieve the best performance at different computation costs, with comprehensive model analyses for better understanding. The proposed HyGA sheds light on a more effective, efficient, and stable attention mechanism.

items.title: LycheeMemory V2: Efficient Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents via Semantic Segment-Level Consolidation
items.description: arXiv:2608.12990v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents must preserve information from past interactions to support future tasks. Existing memory systems typically rely on eager consolidation, invoking LLMs after each interaction to extract, summarize, or update memories. This design makes memory construction increasingly costly as conversations grow. Coarse summarization can reduce construction cost but risks discarding fine-grained contextual evidence, whereas larger retrieval contexts or multi-hop LLM reasoning shift the overhead to query time. We present LycheeMemory V2, an efficient long-term memory framework that replaces turn-level consolidation with semantic segment-level consolidation. Instead of consolidating every interaction, LycheeMemory batches multiple exchanges into segments and encodes each finalized segment into context-independent typed memory records. Segment-level batching lowers LLM encoding frequency, while semantic boundary detection helps preserve coherent event-level and temporal evidence compared with fixed-window batching. The resulting records are organized with lightweight structured indexes for query-planned evidence retrieval. Experiments using GPT-4.1-Mini show that LycheeMemory achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching 89.22% on LoCoMo and 92.20% on LongMemEval-S. Compared with A-Mem, it reduces construction tokens by 86.0% on LoCoMo and 75.9% on LongMemEval-S without increasing query-time token usage. More broadly, our results suggest that the accuracy--cost trade-off of long-term agent memory depends not only on what information is retained, but also on the granularity at which it is consolidated.

items.title: Refusing Intent, Not Form: Wrapper-Based Intent-Group Supervision for LLM Safety
items.description: arXiv:2608.13304v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A common way to improve jailbreak robustness is to train on harmful requests rewritten as role-play, translation, or other forms. When used only for harmful requests, these forms may become refusal shortcuts, weakening unseen-attack robustness and increasing benign over-refusal. We propose Wrapper-Based Intent-Form Augmentation (WIFA), which applies shared wrapper families to harmful and benign requests and groups variants by intent, encouraging decisions based on underlying intent rather than wrapper cues. WIFA supports two independent routes: WIFA-Boost prioritizes safety through two-stage training, while A-GCRT enforces consistent decisions across wrappers to mitigate over-refusal. Across three model families and two harmful training sources, both routes consistently improve safety while largely retaining capability. On Qwen--AdvBench, WIFA-Boost raises SB-avg5 from 22.1\% to 63.7\%, the best among compared methods; A-GCRT raises it to 46.7\% while reducing OR-Bench over-refusal from 25.7\% to 17.4\%, unlike reproduced defenses whose safety gains increase over-refusal. Across three AdvBench-trained backbones, both routes substantially reduce ASR on 15 unseen attack families and under model-adaptive GCG and RandomSearch. Overall, WIFA provides reusable intent-group supervision across models and training sources, supporting high safety through WIFA-Boost and substantial safety gains with less unnecessary refusal through A-GCRT.

items.title: Frozen Memory Is Not Enough: Rethinking External Memory as Extraction
items.description: arXiv:2608.17050v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Methods for improving knowledge use in large language models typically fall into two regimes. Non-parametric retrieval offers flexible access to external knowledge, but adds retrieval latency, context overhead, and only shallow integration with the backbone. Parametric adaptation is efficient at inference time, but entangles knowledge with model weights and can be hard to update, audit, or transfer. Engram-style hashed memory occupies a middle regime: it stores learned information in an external, addressable table, yet consumes that table through a small learned reader. This raises a basic question: when such a memory is moved across backbones, what matters more, the frozen memory itself or the target-side reader? We study this question through cross-model frozen-memory extraction, in which a memory trained on a source model is frozen and attached to a different target model, with only a lightweight reader trained. Ablations show that learned memory content and correct addressing both matter, but the transferred table becomes useful only through a reader aligned to the target model. In downstream question answering tasks, a dual-layer, four-branch reader nearly closes the gap between same-model and cross-model reuse, achieving an average score of 38.8 under our controlled evaluation protocol. Moreover, when the provider reader is directly compatible with the target interface, the frozen artifact can provide substantial utility without target-side training, while optional reader adaptation yields further improvement. These results suggest that Engram can serve as a reusable external knowledge artifact, provided that the target has access to a compatible reader interface; target-side adaptation can further improve alignment when direct reader reuse is insufficient.

items.title: DCGC: Draft-Conditioned Global Correction for Complex Reasoning with Masked Diffusion Models
items.description: arXiv:2608.25428v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Correcting flawed reasoning traces remains a significant challenge for Large Language Models (LLMs), whose autoregressive generation can propagate early mistakes into subsequent reasoning. We introduce DCGC, a Masked Diffusion Model (MDM) framework for global correction that uses an imperfect solution draft from an upstream solver as auxiliary context. DCGC combines task-specific Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with a novel inference-time mechanism called Dynamic Dual-CFG. This mechanism separates problem-only and joint problem-draft branches and scales the draft-conditioned residual using a relative confidence gap. Across math, code, and knowledge reasoning benchmarks, DCGC outperforms standard sampling and simpler CFG variants, with additional results suggesting transfer to different diffusion backbones. In test-time setting where ground-truth failure labels are unavailable, DCGC improves full test set accuracy by correcting low-consensus upstream outputs, highlighting its utility as a verifier-free global correction module for difficult reasoning instances.

items.title: TreeGraft: Adaptive Multi-Drafter Grafting for Tree-Based Speculative Decoding
items.description: arXiv:2608.26112v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through a draft-then-verify paradigm. Building on this, tree-structured methods improve inference by organizing proposals into multiple candidate paths, increasing the accepted length. However, existing tree-structured methods use a single drafter for all drafting steps, creating a dilemma: a smaller drafter is fast but yields lower-quality trees, whereas a larger drafter improves tree quality but suffers from high latency. To address this, we propose TreeGraft, a multi-drafter framework in which drafters of different costs jointly construct a shared draft tree. TreeGraft uses the stronger drafter to rescore candidates by updating scores assigned by the weaker drafter, reselect grafting positions, and recover promising paths left unexplored. It also integrates stronger drafter expansions non-destructively, preserving existing branches that may still be accepted by the target model. Together, these designs improve the quality of the shared draft tree. To control the drafting cost, TreeGraft introduces a lightweight scheduler distilled from an offline value system to decide when to call the stronger drafter. Across 10 model pairs and 6 benchmarks, TreeGraft outperforms the better of the two fixed single-drafter endpoint strategies by 15.1% on average, reaching a maximum gain of 26.6%. Our code is available at https://github.com/fjm9933/TreeGraft.

items.title: BTS-AgentBench: A Deterministic, Replayable Pipeline from Read-Only Telemetry Logs to Agent Benchmarks
items.description: arXiv:2608.27334v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Operational facilities accumulate extensive local telemetry, but agent-ready interactive evaluations with source-verifiable answers are costly to construct from such archives. Site-specific measurement histories also motivate a local conversion workflow that can operate where raw operational data must remain under organizational control. We introduce BTS-AgentBench, a deterministic compiler that transforms read-only telemetry and equipment metadata into tool-backed, multi-turn agent tasks, phase-level targets, evidence and executable evaluation contracts. The BTS release includes 532 episodes across nine families; a second-corpus port produces 204 XAI4HEAT episodes. Frozen-input replay reproduces released artifacts byte-for-byte, and independent raw-source checks cover all 89 BTS and 41 XAI4HEAT test episodes. Replayable provenance links 1,170 trial identities to recorded execution and scorer conditions, while 1,125 completed traces retain model responses and tool results. An obligation-level comparison of 216 scored failures found that linked records exposed additional recorded failed obligations in 202 cases (93.5\%), including tool arguments, stream identity, state carryover and missing interaction steps. The pipeline thereby supports source-grounded task generation, exact reconstruction and auditable diagnosis of agent executions. Code, released benchmarks, and reproduction instructions are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/telemetry-benchmark-reproduction-3D68

items.title: RATIO: A Benchmark for Retrieval Across Typed Ideation Operations in Scientific Literature
items.description: arXiv:2608.27394v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Retrieved scientific literature can serve as inspiration for both human and AI scientists. Inspiration can take different forms: prior work may directly suggest how to address a problem, or surface directions at different levels of abstraction---zooming out to a more general view or zooming in to a concrete realization. We introduce RATIO (Retrieval Across Typed Ideation Operations), a large-scale benchmark in which relevance is defined by three operations which we name ideation moves: Address retrieves potential approaches for stated problems, Broaden retrieves more general formulations, and Specify retrieves concrete instantiations. RATIO is constructed from millions of full-text scientific papers across CS literature via a general recipe that extends discourse-marker distant supervision---previously used only for classification---to corpus-scale retrieval, combined with extensive LLM and human vetting. Experiments show that operation-specific fine-tuning substantially boosts retrievers and LLM reranking helps further, but much room for improvement remains. Researchers blind to condition found the fine-tuned retriever's candidates more useful as inspirations. RATIO provides a scalable training and evaluation framework for retrieval components that support literature-grounded ideation, opening up new research avenues in scientific inspiration retrieval. We release full data, code, models, and annotations.

items.title: Lazy Grounding: Attacking Search Agents with Factual Evidence
items.description: arXiv:2608.30303v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Search agents mitigate hallucination by grounding their answers in retrieved web results. However, retrieval-based approaches also introduce an attack surface: agents may cite misinformation from poisoned search corpora containing false or malicious documents. We demonstrate that, in some cases, search agents' reasoning and responses may be steered by completely factual but distracting information. We refer to this failure as lazy grounding. We expose lazy grounding by injecting nearby evidence from answer-changing rewrites of benchmark questions into the search corpora. Each document contains factual evidence that supports a neighboring rewritten question but is retrieved for the original question. Across 12 model-benchmark pairs, the attack causes the accuracy of search agents' responses to drop by 5.9 points on average and by up to 17.3 points, while inducing nearby-answer adoption in every setting. The effect is even stronger when nearby evidence appears later or is more answer-shaped. Our results show that robust search agents must defend against not only misinformation but also the misapplication of factual evidence. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/frankyzha/lazy-grounding.

items.title: Reviser: Writing and Editing Text with Autoregressive Cursor Actions
items.description: arXiv:2609.20830v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language models write text once, left to right, and models that write in other orders, such as diffusion LMs, pay for it with many full-sequence passes. We introduce Reviser, a decoder-only Transformer that writes and edits text with cursor actions (insert, move, delete, stop) that a deterministic executor applies to a canvas. Reviser is autoregressive over its own actions, so a step costs the same as an autoregressive (AR) step. We train Reviser to continue text, including a self-correction recipe that types a wrong token and deletes it, and Reviser-Edit to revise a draft, and compare each with a same-size AR model trained on the same data, using three LLM judges on continuations cut to the same length. Reviser-Edit beats its matched AR rewriter on CoEdIT SARI (+7.2 at 100M, +4.5 at 300M; two seeds agree) with a third of the decoding steps and latency, though the AR rewriter corrects grammar better. In continuation, Reviser beats diffusion LMs of similar size (62-74% win rate) at a fraction of their compute; two of three judges prefer its AR twin, and one slightly prefers Reviser at 100M. Reviser fills gaps it left and backspaces a just-typed repeated token with probability 0.85-0.87.

items.title: An Iterative LangGraph Agent for Text-to-SQL: Natural Language Access to the Chicago Crime Database
items.description: arXiv:2609.22917v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Non-technical stakeholders frequently cannot write the SQL needed to extract insights from operational databases. We built and evaluated a Text-to-SQL agent that closes this gap end to end: a six-node LangGraph StateGraph checks question relevance, fetches the live schema, generates PostgreSQL, validates it with a dry run, retries on failure, executes the query, and narrates the result set in plain English. The agent uses prompt engineering only; no model was fine-tuned. We evaluated it on the Chicago Crime dataset (approximately 8.5 million records, 22 attributes) against a hand-built benchmark of 100 natural language questions with ground-truth SQL, stratified into 30 Easy, 40 Medium and 30 Hard items. Comparing two prompt revisions of the same agent, the revised system (V2) reached a Valid SQL Rate of 93% (from 87%), an Execution Accuracy of 60% under a hybrid relational equivalence metric (from 47%; 19% from 12% under strict JSON matching), and a mean Synthesis Quality of 4.34 out of 5 (from 3.91). The single largest driver was removing a LIMIT 10 instruction from the system prompt, which had been truncating multi-row answers. Error analysis attributes the residual failures to relevance-checker false rejections, ambiguous question semantics, and free-tier API rate limits rather than to the language generation step. We report no comparison against an external baseline system or a public benchmark; the study is a single-model engineering evaluation.

items.title: ARAFA: An LLM-Generated Arabic Fact-Checking Dataset
items.description: arXiv:2609.25833v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automatic fact-checking poses a significant challenge in Arabic natural language processing due to the scarcity of datasets and resources. In this manuscript, we introduce Arafa, a new large-scale dataset for fact-checking in Modern Standard Arabic, constructed through an automated framework leveraging large language models (LLMs). The dataset was constructed through a three-step pipeline: (1) claim generation from Arabic Wikipedia pages with supporting textual evidence, (2) claim mutation to generate challenging counterfactual claims with refuting evidence, and (3) an automatic validation step to validate that the generated claims are either supported or refuted by their accompanying evidence, or if the evidence does not provide enough information to judge the validity of the claims. The resulting dataset comprises 181,976 claim-evidence pairs labeled as supported, refuted, or not enough information. Human evaluation carried out on a test sample from the dataset demonstrated strong inter-annotator agreement (kappa = 0.89) using Cohen's Kappa for supported claims and (kappa = 0.94) for refuted claims. Automatic validation based on a human-evaluated sample achieved 86% accuracy for supported claims and 88% for refuted ones. To showcase Arafa's value as a resource for automatic Arabic fact-checking, four open-source transformer-based models were fine-tuned using Arafa, with the top-performing model achieving a Macro F1-score of 77% on the test data. In addition to Arafa being the first large-scale dataset for Arabic fact-checking, our framework presents a scalable approach for developing similar resources for other low-resource languages.

items.title: MemoryAthena: Adaptive Routing over Latent and Generated Memories
items.description: arXiv:2609.25853v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learned-memory methods store information in an explicit table and consume it through a separate reader, allowing addressing, storage, and reading to be modified independently. We study whether useful memory can also be generated rather than only retrieved. MemoryAthena uses three pathways: direct Engram retrieval (E), generation from retrieved Engram cues (GE), and generation from causal backbone states without consulting the memory table (GH). Generated memory is conditionally useful: it can complement E in one context but interfere with it in another. MemoryAthena therefore treats E as an anchor and learns when a generated representation should intervene. With the backbone, memory, generators, and readers frozen, a lightweight causal routing head is trained from counterfactual future-token likelihood advantages of GE and GH relative to E. At inference time, an admitted candidate modifies the E residual through bounded interpolation, while rejection recovers the direct pathway exactly. On question answering, MemoryAthena raises the five-task average from 37.65 to 39.28 over the direct pathway of the same checkpoint, while the six-task general-NLP average increases from 76.73 to 79.13. The complete memory-side system contains approximately 201M parameters, excluding the frozen backbone. Further analyses show complementary strengths among E, GE, and GH across tasks and inputs. These results support generated memory as a selective correction to direct retrieval and highlight routing when, which, and how strongly to intervene as the central challenge.

items.title: EduBehaviors: Assertion-based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues
items.description: arXiv:2609.27043v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models have enabled rapid deployment of language classification and analysis, allowing users to describe complex constructs in natural language, such as pedagogical moves or expressions of learning and engagement, and label them in conversational datasets such as classroom or tutoring transcripts. However, because LLM reasoning is opaque, we have no verifiable, mechanistic insight into why a model chose a label for an utterance, and output differences over time or across models challenge replication. We introduce the EduBehaviors framework to generate interpretable, reliable, and scalable construct annotations in educational dialogue data that retain human agency while leveraging the strengths of generative AI, encoders, and machine learning models. We evaluate the framework on the TalkMoves dataset, predicting the Teacher TalkMoves labels. Our best configuration results in a macro-F1 of 0.764 and 0.756 Cohen's kappa, demonstrating improvements over direct prompting approaches and showing competitiveness with fine-tuned classifiers while gaining the benefit of greater transparency and comparability. To facilitate adoption and operationalization of the EduBehaviors framework in educational dialogue data by other researchers, we also release the EduBehaviors Toolkit with two complementary open-source tools based on the TalkMoves application.

items.title: Policy-Conditioned AI-Use Detection: An Evidentiary Framework for Academic Publishing
items.description: arXiv:2609.38427v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Major venues now publish detailed rules about how authors, reviewers, and area chairs may use AI, and those rules differ by role, by task, and by what must be disclosed. AI detection, the instrument usually proposed to enforce them, estimates something else: whether an AI model wrote the text. We argue that this target is misaligned with the decisions conferences and journals face, and propose policy-conditioned AI-use detection, an evidentiary framework for assessing whether a human--AI workflow complied with a stated rule. Policy makes the governing rule an explicit input. Inference reports hypotheses, evidence, calibration regime, and uncertainty in place of verdicts such as "AI detected". Evaluation builds benchmarks from reproducible pipelines that generate compliant and non-compliant workflows, and reports true positive rate at a false positive rate the venue fixes in advance. We work the framework through peer review, where at plausible violation rates a detector at a strong operating point still flags more compliant authors than violating ones. The framework therefore also names what a venue must instrument: structured disclosure, approved-tool routing that respects reviewer confidentiality, and a path by which a finding can be contested. Under this framing a detector is not an authorship classifier but an auditable procedure with an error rate the venue fixes in advance and can defend.

items.title: Old Ideas, Novel Problems: The Instability of LLM-Based Novelty Evaluation
items.description: arXiv:2610.02022v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI-based ideation systems are often evaluated on the novelty of their ideas, and that judgment is increasingly delegated to large language models. Such judges are typically built ad hoc and validated, if at all, on human-authored papers rather than on the generated ideas they are meant to score. So, how do novelty judges perform? Not well. We present a systematic controlled study of novelty evaluation design choices. We build an evaluation set automatically, mining OpenReview for passages where reviewers explicitly affirm or dispute a paper's originality and keeping only submissions with unanimous agreement at the extremes of their research area; we pair these with ideas from a vanilla LLM generator. Across six judges, we find that seemingly small prompt design choices have large consequences; e.g., simply telling the judge that reviewers found one idea novel and the other not can change its verdict on more than half of the identical idea pairs it is shown, shifting pairwise accuracy by over 50 points and occasionally pushing it below chance. The same change helps one judge and hurts another. Retrieval and larger reasoning budgets help little, and two purpose-built novelty evaluators are outperformed by our cheapest prompted baseline. These results raise questions about reported novelty gains of automated ideation systems, and call for robust novelty evaluation methods.

items.title: Quality-Aware Self-Correcting Speech Translation on an Edge Device
