Laws are a priori; data provide instances. Inference is geometric evolution under law constraints. We organize symplectic geometry, GENERIC, kernel methods, RKHS, group-equivariant networks, and constrained mechanics into a unified, analyzable, implementable, verifiable framework. We propose the SKG octuple S = (M, g, omega, H, S, G, Delta, Pi), whose four components correspond to four levels of laws: conservation laws, constitutive relations, symmetry groups, and axiom systems. Main results: (1) Invariants enter metric construction via the Jacobian: g = J^T Sigma^-1 J + epsilon_G I. For constant cases, we establish inverse reconstruction theory: solvability rank condition (Thm 3.9), consistency criterion (Thm 3.11), and uniqueness theorem (Thm 3.14). (2) The kernel bandwidth matrix is uniquely determined by Fisher information and satisfies task-independence (Thm 3.19). (3) The metric reconstruction error decomposes into four terms (Thm 3.21), with squared condition number kappa(Sigma^*)^2 as the dominant amplification factor (Thm 3.22). (4) For state-dependent cases, we establish function-space reconstruction theory on matrix-valued RKHS (Thms 4.8, 4.9). (5) Three-layer projections handle axiom, symplectic-step, and conservation constraints. (6) The residual equation yields the observable formula, four-dimensional rank condition, and noise propagation, while g_qq is structurally unidentifiable. (7) Kernel parameterization yields the RKHS extrapolation bound (Thm 4.15) and strict OOD gain theorem in group directions (Thm 8.15). (8) The learning-decoupling theorem (Thm 9.1) proves the sole object of induction is the parameters of the task energy. Validation: 1D damped oscillator and 2D rotation-invariant system; 6 unit tests, 10 experiments (paired t-test, p < 0.01).

items.title: CktHGVAE: A Symmetric Design/State Heterogeneous Graph Variational Autoencoder for Transistor-level Analog/Mixed-signal Circuit Design and Analysis
items.description: arXiv:2610.19508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose CktHGVAE, a heterogeneous graph variational autoencoder for transistor-level analog/mixedsignal CMOS circuits that takes not only design variables but also state variables as its inputs and outputs. With a single hyperparameter configuration without topology-specific tuning, comparison between model-generated and SPICE-simulated circuit operational states gives median R2 values above 0.9 for typical single-ended voltage amplifiers and the CMOS inverter, and 0.81-0.96 for differential amplifiers with larger datasets. Latent-space optimization in the PCA-reduced latent space with Bayesian optimization, evolutionary search, random search, and quasi-exhaustive search is demonstrated for a common-source voltage amplifier with NMOS input and resistive load, where the objective function is defined as a penalty for deviation from required circuit specifications. For each search strategy, 93.3 - 100% of all design candidates suggested by the model satisfy the required circuit specifications at the decoder output, and SPICE simulations verify that 90 - 100% of them indeed satisfy the requirements. The model pretrained on a batch of topologies can be transferred to unseen topologies without retraining at all, with zero-shot reconstruction median R2 values of 0.72-0.90 in three of four scenarios, including transfer from single-ended to differential topologies, although the transfer fidelity depends on the choice of pretraining topologies. Our demonstrations suggest that the proposed model can potentially serve as a basis for AMS CMOS circuit design automation.

items.title: HankelKANet: Lightweight Path Loss Estimation via Physics-Inspired Hankel Convolution
items.description: arXiv:2610.19524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate path loss (PL) estimation is essential for wireless network planning and optimization. This paper proposes HankelKANet, a lightweight physics-inspired network for PL estimation that structurally embeds electromagnetic propagation characteristics into the neural architecture. Built on a single residual UNet backbone, the proposed model integrates urban layout features with a convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold network(KAN). Specifically, the convolutional kernels are parameterized by the radial amplitudes of the zeroth- and first-order Hankel functions. This formulation acts as a physics-inspired nonlinear distance encoding, enabling the network to capture dominant attenuation characteristics directly without requiring additional physics-based loss terms. Experimental results demonstrate that HankelKANet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency on both the simulated RadioMapSeer dataset and the real-world Huawei RSRPSet. Compared with the leading baseline, PEFNet, it reduces the parameter count by 78% and lowers the RMSE by 16.96% on the simulated data, while further exhibiting robust cross-dataset transferability and high data efficiency during target-domain adaptation. To interpret these empirical gains, we mathematically establish a parameter-conditional spatial gradient bound. Using discrete Dirichlet energy (DDE) and Jacobian sensitivity heatmaps, we empirically verify that this physical encoding intrinsically constrains the network's spatial derivatives. This structural smoothness effectively eliminates non-physical spatial ripples, preventing overfitting to simulator artifacts and serving as the fundamental driver for robust real world generalization.

items.title: Two-stage Residual Learning for Modelling Strength-Informed Optimisation of Thermal Systems
items.description: arXiv:2610.19539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aggregate performance metrics do not identify local modelling inaccuracies in machine learning (ML) surrogates used for thermal-system optimisation. This study assesses local modelling strength through validation-based reliability screening and post-optimisation residual assessment. A two-stage residual learning (TSRL) framework, built on artificial neural networks (ANNs), is developed for modelling-strength-informed and domain-constrained optimisation of thermal systems. Within the TSRL framework, a base ANN predicts the process output, and a residual ANN learns the signed residuals left by the base ANN. The TSRL framework is implemented on two case studies of thermal systems, including 817 simulation observations of a crude distillation unit and operating records from a 395 MW industrial gas turbine. The TSRL framework reduces the test root mean square error (RMSE) from 10.3 g/s to 4.7 g/s for Fuel Oil in the refinery dataset and from 151 kJ/kWh to 105 kJ/kWh for turbine heat rate (THR). The base ANNs trained within TSRL are embedded in domain-constrained optimisation problems, and the modelling strength at each computed solution is assessed using the locked residual-score threshold. Each computed solution receives a good modelled region (GMR) or weak modelled region (WMR) label to inform ML model-based decision-making for safety-critical operation of thermal systems.

items.title: Test-Time Forecasting: Recurrent Depth Enables In-Context Dynamics Prediction
items.description: arXiv:2610.19552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundation models for dynamical systems can forecast unseen partial differential equations (PDEs), ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and time series during inference. However, it remains an open question whether these foundation models truly learn generalizable in-context forecasting strategies. We show that looped transformers are capable of emulating propagators for dynamical systems in-context by first establishing a link between linear attention and (extended) dynamic mode decomposition. We then generalize this insight into the $\textit{Test-Time Forecasting}$ (TTF) framework in which a one-step forecaster leverages iterations of gradient descent as recurrent depth. We demonstrate that lightweight TTF models trained on ODEs and PDEs generalize to out-of-distribution system dynamics during autoregressive rollout after being trained for one-step prediction. Our results reinforce TTF as a theoretically motivated framework for designing recurrent depth models capable of forecasting unseen dynamical systems at test-time.

items.title: TEX-MEX: Similarity-Guided Temporal Contrastive Learning for Time Series
items.description: arXiv:2610.19557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Contrastive learning for time series depends on deciding which pairs of inputs should be treated as similar and dissimilar. Because few augmentations reliably preserve meaning in time series, prior methods have relied on two disjoint notions of similarity between windows: structural similarity, which relates windows with similar morphology, and temporal similarity, which relates windows that occur close together in time. We introduce TEX-MEX, to our knowledge the first approach to unify the two into a single relationship. Given a random batch of windows drawn across the dataset, TEX-MEX uses the encoder to identify which windows are structurally similar or dissimilar to each other. It then pulls each window toward the temporally shifted versions of similar windows and pushes it away from those of dissimilar ones, learning what typically accompanies similar windows in time. Across PPG, EEG, ECG, accelerometry, and continuous glucose monitoring, TEX-MEX broadly achieves state-of-the-art performance against contrastive, reconstructive, JEPA-based, and modality-specific approaches, establishing it as a strong general SSL objective. We further train a 560K-parameter PPG foundation model that achieves state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of downstream benchmarks while being roughly 50x smaller than the next-best unimodally pretrained PPG foundation model in our evaluation. We will release this foundation model open-source and open-weight to the community to support future work and practical applications.

items.title: Learning Across Temporal Graph Representation Silos
items.description: arXiv:2610.19576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal graph data are recorded in different representations, but whether these differences also determine the scope of learned knowledge reuse remains unclear. This study investigates whether predictive structure learned from relational histories can be reused between continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) and temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs). Bidirectional reuse emerges while retaining distinct input and prediction interfaces and independent vocabularies, and sources with the same representation are not always more useful. Controlled reorganizations of source histories show that the organization contributing to reuse varies across source-target conditions. We show that learned aspects of Relational Dynamics, the predictive structure present in relational histories, can be reused across conventional representation boundaries. Independently pretrained TKG and CTDG learners can also be fused at the score level to improve prediction on a third dataset without entity or relation-semantic alignment. Two proofs of concept in recommendation and security detection illustrate that external temporal sources without direct alignment can also become useful pretraining resources.

items.title: InstructPro2: Natural Language and Biological Grounding Guided De Novo Protein Design
items.description: arXiv:2610.19592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ability to generate proteins with desired functions is a central goal of computational biology. Although natural language can express diverse design objectives, existing protein generation methods often support only narrow tasks or make limited use of biological constraints. We develop InstructPro2 to translate natural-language design objectives into protein sequences while incorporating task-specific biological context. A text encoder captures the design instructions, while dedicated ligand and antigen encoders provide biological context to the sequence-generating decoder. For pretraining, we assemble InstructPro2Bench, comprising 205.7 million pairs from UniProtKB. We subsequently adapt the model to ligand-binding protein and antibody design. On functional protein generation benchmarks, InstructPro2 outperforms Pinal, the strongest baseline, achieving a functional recovery F1 of 74.8 versus 62.2 and lowering global RMSD from 5.33A to 3.04A. For antibody design, the model obtains a DockQ score of 0.39, while ligand-binding protein design reaches a docking success rate of 72.6%. These findings highlight how integrating language-based instructions with biological conditioning can extend protein generation to distinct design settings.

items.title: Beyond Static Positional Encoding: Bayesian Time-aware Attention for Non-Stationary Long-term Time Series Forecasting
items.description: arXiv:2610.19603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformers have demonstrated strong performance in long-term time series forecasting (LTSF), yet modeling non-stationary temporal dependencies remains challenging. In this paper, we interpret self-attention as a Bayesian posterior over attended positions, combining a content-based prior induced by scaled dot-product similarity with a temporal-evidence likelihood induced by positional encoding. This formulation provides a probabilistic interpretation of how positional encoding shapes the temporal dependencies captured by self-attention. Building on this perspective, we derive a population-level evidence lower bound (ELBO) that characterizes the role of positional encoding in forecasting weakly stationary time series. Our analysis further highlights a limitation of static positional encoding: when temporal dependence structures vary across input windows, a fixed temporal bias must accommodate heterogeneous dynamics and can therefore be suboptimal for non-stationary forecasting. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Bayesian Time-aware Attention (BTA), which employs a mixture-of-experts (MoE) router to adaptively combine temporal kernels and generate input-conditioned, head-specific positional biases. Extensive experiments on standard LTSF benchmarks demonstrate that BTA consistently improves forecasting performance across multiple Transformer backbones and achieves competitive overall performance with modest computational overhead and stable training.

items.title: Synthetic reaction data from transformation rules for graph-to-sequence pretraining in biodegradation pathway prediction
items.description: arXiv:2610.19640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The scarcity of observed biodegradation reactions constrains the training of product and pathway predictors. We present enviGraph, a framework that generates and curates synthetic reaction data, uses these data to pretrain a graph-to-sequence predictor, and fine-tunes the predictor on observed environmental reactions for product and recursive pathway prediction. Applying inherited environmental transformation rules to structures from PubChem, NORMAN SusDat and EPA DSSTox, followed by curation, produces 776,851 canonical parent-product pairs for pretraining. We compare this dataset with three United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) reaction datasets: USPTO-50K, USPTO-MIT and USPTO-Stereo. We evaluate enviGraph and the sequence-based enviFormer using ten folds split by pathway on the EAWAG Biocatalysis/Biodegradation Database (BBD), regulatory pesticide biodegradation data (Soil) and activated-sludge biodegradation data (Sludge). For both predictors, synthetic pretraining gives the highest BBD mean precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) among the evaluated pretraining datasets for single-generation and multi-generation prediction. enviGraph achieves BBD single-generation PR-AUC of $0.202 \pm 0.050$ with synthetic pretraining, compared with $0.169 \pm 0.065$ for the retrospectively selected strongest USPTO condition, USPTO-Stereo (mean $\pm$ sample standard deviation across folds). Its exact BBD top-1 and top-5 accuracies with synthetic pretraining are 0.355 and 0.594. The strongest USPTO conditions give higher PR-AUC means than synthetic pretraining in most Soil and Sludge comparisons. enviGraph has higher Soil multi-generation PR-AUC means than enviFormer under each of the four main pretraining datasets, and with synthetic pretraining it also leads enviFormer on BBD single-generation PR-AUC and exact top-1 and top-5 accuracy.

items.title: On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization
items.description: arXiv:2610.19652v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work has sought to transfer first-order nonconvex optimization guarantees to zeroth-order methods through gradient estimators, typically incurring a factor linear in $d$. \citet{kornowski2024} obtained an $\mathcal{O}(d\delta^{-1}\epsilon^{-3})$ oracle complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization and asked whether its dependence on all three parameters is jointly optimal. Although the dimension dependence and the first-order dependence on $(\delta,\epsilon)$ are separately known to be unavoidable, a matching zeroth-order lower bound has remained open. We answer this question in the unrestricted full-space setting. For smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization, we establish a scalar-oracle lower bound of $\Omega\!\left(dL_0^2\min\{\Delta H,L_0^2\}/\epsilon^4\right)$ assuming a smooth, globally lower-bounded population objective and a second-moment bound on sample Lipschitz constants. A smooth reduction then yields a lower bound for Goldstein stationarity, proving the joint minimax optimality of the dependence on $(d,\delta,\epsilon)$ under explicit high-dimensional and small-accuracy conditions. Crucially, our results allow algorithms to query arbitrary points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, adaptively select sample-function labels, reuse the same sampled function at any number of locations, and output points without spatial restrictions. Thus, unlike lower bounds based on bounded query regions or fresh evaluation noise, our guarantees apply to a fully adaptive, reusable-sample scalar oracle. We also establish a separate noiseless exact-value lower bound against randomized algorithms, and hence also against deterministic methods. Our proof combines a globally defined sequential nonconvex construction with an exact Gaussian scalar channel, multistage random-field estimates, and an antithetic finite-sample realization that preserves information hardness under adaptive reuse.

items.title: Enhancing Latent World Models with Associative Memory
items.description: arXiv:2610.19683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models trained via latent dynamics offer a scalable path for embodied planning, yet existing methods suffer from representational collapse, computational overhead, and limited long-horizon capability. We introduce a memory-enhanced latent world model that augments JEPA-style prediction with a content-addressable memory bank. Our approach learns high-level representations directly from observations, operating at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, and conditions predictions via adaptive layer normalization. To prevent collapse and ensure effective memory usage, we design two complementary losses that encourage slot diversity and balanced temporal utilization. Experiments on PushT, Tworoom, Reacher, and OGBCube demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight architecture, outperforming conventional latent world models on long-horizon planning tasks.

items.title: Annealed L\'{e}vy Diffusion via Gaussian Surrogate Reverse Dynamics
items.description: arXiv:2610.19692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gaussian diffusion models offer a practical framework for generative modeling. Denoising L\'{e}vy Probabilistic Models (DLPM) introduce heavy-tailed perturbations with a fixed tail index throughout denoising. We introduce Annealed L\'{e}vy Diffusion (ALD). ALD varies the stability index $\alpha(t)$ to combine heavy-tailed exploration with Gaussian refinement. Our marginal-first formulation represents stable noise as a scalar Gaussian scale mixture. This formulation enables standard Gaussian noise-prediction training with one additional scale input. We study two sampling processes. ALD-renoise estimates the clean sample and injects fresh marginal noise. ALD-posterior preserves dependence between successive states through an accumulated conditional variance and a Gaussian bridge update. Both samplers reuse the same trained predictor with different scalar inputs. We evaluate ALD on four 2D benchmarks and an imbalanced nine-mode mixture. We also examine training efficiency and the effects of prediction perturbations on clipped Holtsmark data. Additional experiments evaluate MNIST and CelebA64 generation and CIFAR-10LT augmentation. ALD preserves local geometry on the evaluated light-tailed and manifold-structured targets.

items.title: ReGRA: Residual-Gradient Adaptation for Complementary Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
items.description: arXiv:2610.19700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao-Li/ReGRA.

items.title: New Model, Old Habits: Behavior Transfer under Model Swapping in Multi-Session LLM Agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.19712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-session agents can switch between LLMs to balance performance and inference cost. Such switches require transferring a history for continuity, yet their effects on the recipient remain underexplored. Through controlled experiments with multi-session tasks, we uncover behavior transfer: recipients tend to adopt reasoning and action patterns from the models that generated their histories. This effect is most evident with raw-history transfer but is substantially reduced by summarization. Based on these findings, we propose Direction- and Authorship-aware Summarization of History (DASH) that preserves stronger-model behavior while minimizing weak-to-strong transfer via summarization. Experiments with repeated swaps show that DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines. These results suggest that effective multi-model orchestration requires considering not only which model to use, but also which behavioral patterns to carry forward.

items.title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
items.description: arXiv:2610.19731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.

items.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
items.description: arXiv:2610.19738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.

items.title: CAST: History-Adaptive Spectral Clipping for LLM Pretraining
items.description: arXiv:2610.19761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Soft spectral clipping (SSC) reduces gradient singular values, but its effect depends on the gradient scale and clipping threshold. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), a history-adaptive extension of SSC. AdamW's previous second moment sets row and column scales. An exponential moving average of the clipped output's estimated spectral norm sets each matrix's threshold. CAST restores the original coordinates before the AdamW update. We train a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 19.08B total parameters for 83.89B tokens. CAST achieves lower training and mean validation losses than nine gradient-processing baselines, with the fewest relative gradient spikes. It reaches the best baseline's final smoothed training loss in 7.2\% fewer steps.

items.title: Learning to Compute Is Not Learning to Retain or Reuse in Looped Transformers
items.description: arXiv:2610.19768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped transformers compute by applying one block repeatedly, so they can run for more loops than they were trained with. Recurrent reasoners are known to overthink: iterating past the trained depth can turn a correct answer into a wrong one. Such a late error can reflect failed computation, loss of retention, or a state that later computation cannot reuse. We separate these cases in in-context Mealy-machine execution, where a simulator supplies intermediate targets and exact counterfactuals for hidden-state interventions. Models trained to answer at loop 32 are fully correct there but keep only 22% of these answers at loop 64. Retention depends on what training asks for: supervising one randomly chosen position per example, instead of always the last, keeps 99.8%, and randomizing the number of training loops also helps; truncating gradients, as in progressive training against overthinking, does not. The computation itself is exact: position $k$ is computed at loop $k$, and swapping its loop-$k$ hidden vector for the one from another input redirects every later position to that input's exact continuation (237/237 pairs in each of ten models). Retention, however, is not reuse. Even in models that keep nearly all answers, holding each position $k$ fixed from loop $k$ drops accuracy to 4--6%, whereas holding it from loop $k+4$ is harmless. A released recurrent maze network trained to avoid overthinking behaves the same way. Learning to compute is thus not learning to retain, and avoiding overthinking does not make a state reusable when its answer first appears.

items.title: From Global to Tail Convergence: Dynamics of $\alpha$-Stable Score-Based Generative Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.19773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Score-based generative models driven by $\alpha$-stable L{\'e}vy processes have been proposed as an alternative to Brownian diffusion models, with empirical evidence suggesting improved sampling and better modeling of heavy-tailed data. Yet theoretical guarantees for these models remain limited. We develop a non-asymptotic convergence analysis for scale-preserving $\alpha$-stable generative dynamics, covering both compactly supported and power-law targets. In p-Wasserstein distance, we quantify the effects of early stopping, initialization, score approximation, and time discretization, and show exponential decay of the initialization error. A comparison with Brownian dynamics reveals that global Wasserstein convergence alone does not fundamentally distinguish the two models: both initialization errors decay exponentially with the forward horizon on the common class of heavy-tailed targets. A sharp separation emerges instead in the tails. At any positive generation time, stable dynamics produces power-law tails with index $\alpha$, whereas Brownian dynamics remains light-tailed. For a target with tail index $\nu$, asymptotically correct extreme-quantile scaling is possible precisely when $\alpha$=$\nu$. These results identify tail-index matching as a principled mechanism behind the ability of stable generative models to capture extreme events.

items.title: Learning Who Benefits Most: Multi-Treatment Causal Ranking for Population Health Stratification
items.description: arXiv:2610.19782v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Population health stratification frameworks, such as the Italian DM77, organize patients by clinical need and care pathways but offer limited guidance on which care changes to prioritize under constrained resources. We present PROMETHEUS (Proactive Resource Optimization through Multi-treatment Effect-based Targeting in Healthcare Environments Using Stratification), a framework that formulates population health stratification as a multi-treatment causal ranking problem. Its objective is to order eligible patient-treatment opportunities by expected incremental benefit rather than obtain perfectly calibrated individual treatment-effect estimates. Each clinically admissible care intensification is compared with maintaining the patient's current pathway. Treatments are learned jointly to produce a globally comparable ranking across patients and care profiles, within domains sharing a reference condition, outcome, follow-up horizon, and benefit scale. This separates clinical need, treatment benefit, and resource-constrained allocation. PROMETHEUS combines doubly robust causal signals with a Siamese neural ranking model and contrastive representation pretraining. The shared representation captures similarities across care transitions, supporting prioritization under capacity constraints. Synthetic experiments and semi-synthetic experiments using real administrative covariates from ASL Benevento evaluate ranking quality, allocation value, robustness, and failure modes. The results support the framework's ability to recover generated benefit orderings and prioritize care opportunities in the evaluated settings. PROMETHEUS provides a preclinical approach to actionable stratification; validation with observed treatment-outcome data is required before clinical use.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning via Advantage Guidance
items.description: arXiv:2610.19783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning a policy that can outperform what is shown in the data. However, in practice, such systems suffer from instability and hyperparameter sensitivity. In contrast, supervised learning provides a stable and scalable training objective, but is fundamentally limited by the quality of the demonstrated behavior. In this paper, we ask whether we can perform policy optimization with something as simple and stable as supervised learning but as performant as RL. Unfortunately, naively training the policy with supervised learning and conditioning on future rewards or advantages typically underperform dedicated RL methods. We introduce a new policy extraction method, Advantage Guidance, that retains the simple supervised learning structure with advantage conditioning while outperforming prior RL methods through effective conditional training and contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling. We show that Advantage Guidance can significantly improve a model's ability to respond to conditional advantage signals, and the contrastive guidance during sampling can use the learned advantage-conditioned policy to target the KL-regularized optimal policy. Empirically, we find that Advantage Guidance significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods on 26 long-horizon, sparse reward tasks across datasets with varying degrees of optimality.

items.title: Asymptotically Exact Negative Guidance of Diffusion Models via Positive-Unlabeled Learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.19802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Negative guidance of diffusion models generates samples that avoid an undesired condition, specified either by reference samples or by a conditional score alongside an unconditional model. Existing methods inject repulsive terms derived from local information at each sample, so the resulting sampler does not target an explicit density, and its bias cannot be systematically reduced by increasing computation. We instead present a negative-guidance method that samples from an explicit target density, which uniformly handles both reference-sample and score-based specifications and suppresses probability mass near the undesired condition with an avoidance strength that parametrizes the target density itself. Realizing this target requires estimating, at each diffusion timestep, how likely each sample is to belong to the undesired condition. We cast this estimation as a Positive-Unlabeled learning problem that admits lightweight online training along the diffusion trajectory, using condition samples as positives and diffusion particles as unlabeled data. Because the guided particles drift from the unconditional marginal, we further correct the residual mismatch via Sequential Monte Carlo, yielding a sampler that is asymptotically exact in the particle limit and that turns any existing negative-guidance method into its proposal kernel. Empirically, our method approaches the ground-truth target on Gaussian mixtures and Pareto-dominates existing methods on trade-offs between avoidance and generation quality, distributional bias, and diversity, including in an image-generation setting with a pretrained score network.

items.title: Efficient contextual partial monitoring with general function approximation
items.description: arXiv:2610.19804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study finite stochastic partial monitoring (PM) games with side information, a paradigm of sequential learning with partial feedback. On each round $t \in [T]$, both player and environment observe a context and player chooses an action and environment simultaneously chooses an outcome. The player neither observes the outcome nor the loss; instead, they only observe a feedback symbol which is partially informative about the outcome. We utilize the Estimation-to-Decisions (E2D) meta-algorithm of Foster et al.(2021) to design E2D.PMSide, a computationally efficient framework for contextual partial monitoring, which uses an online regression oracle to efficiently estimate the outcome distributions based on historical (context, action, feedback symbol) tuples. Since the exploration rule given by the original E2D algorithm is intractable to compute, we propose two computationally efficient exploration rules that achieve optimal regret orders in $T$: in the globally observable setting, our exploration rule is based on $\epsilon$-greedy, while in the locally observable setting, our exploration rule uses inverse gap weighting (Foster & Rakhlin, 2020), which was previously only known to be effective in the bandit setting. We show that a variant of E2D.PMSide named OE2D.PMSide can be combined with offline regression oracles to give an efficient algorithm with optimal regret when the contexts are drawn independently from a fixed distribution. We evaluate our algorithm on a synthetic label-efficient prediction game and an LLM routing task, in which a learner decides from prompt, uncertainty, and internal state features whether to escalate a query from a weak model to a strong one. We show that our method has superior performance to prior approaches.

items.title: VaryST: Generalizable Spatio-Temporal Forecasting Beyond the Closed-World Setting
items.description: arXiv:2610.19813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatio-temporal forecasting is fundamental to many real-world systems, yet deployment environments are inherently varying: temporal distributions may evolve, spatial domains may change, and observation availability may shift from training conditions. Existing models are often tightly coupled to their training environments through node-specific representations, predefined spatial support sets, and reliance on consistently available observations, limiting generalization to changing environments. To this end, we propose VaryST, a compact spatio-temporal forecasting model trained from scratch that achieves strong generalization by dynamically constructing predictive context from available long-term observations. To accommodate temporal changes, VaryST derives node representations from long-term histories, capturing current behavior in the context of longer-term patterns. To adapt to spatial changes, it dynamically selects functionally relevant support nodes beyond predefined neighborhoods and integrates their information with recent and long-term target states and global context. To handle varying observation availability, VaryST selectively masks historical patches on which the model relies most during training, encouraging it to exploit alternative temporal and spatial dependencies for accurate forecasting when key observations become unavailable. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets against seventeen baselines show that VaryST achieves strong in-domain forecasting accuracy, substantially improves zero- and few-shot generalization under spatial and temporal changes, and remains robust to varying observation availability.

items.title: When Does Depth Help? Understanding Layerwise Inference in Tabular Foundation Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.19814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformer-based tabular foundation models (TFMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on small to medium-sized tabular prediction tasks while processing diverse inputs through a shared stack of layers. Recent layerwise analyses identify strong predictive performance in early TFM representations and substantial overlap in computation across layers. However, early predictive accessibility alone does not establish whether later layers are dispensable for every input, and aggregate accuracy can obscure which inputs benefit from additional computation. We study all 24 in-context-learning layers of TabPFN-3 across 272 classification datasets, combining representation geometry, prediction trajectories, truncation, and structural interventions, while also examining related representation dynamics in four additional TFMs. We uncover a pronounced expansion-compression trajectory, with stronger late dimensional contraction associated with larger increases in class-prototype separation. A targeted analysis of early-stabilizing samples shows that substantial representational changes persist after predicted classes stabilize, while locally ambiguous queries obtain larger accuracy gains from shallow to late layers than well-separated queries. Repeating a single pretrained block or perturbing layer order reduces predictive performance on average, constraining simple post-hoc substitutions in the frozen model. These findings distinguish predictive accessibility, class stability, and the benefits of continuing computation, supporting an input-dependent assessment of depthwise redundancy in TFMs.

items.title: CTIA-ODE: Continuous-Time Inter-Variable Attention for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
items.description: arXiv:2610.19831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although multivariate time series forecasting has broad application prospects, effectively incorporating exogenous variables remains challenging. Prevailing discrete-time architectures often impose rigid temporal alignment across heterogeneous variables, which may limit their ability to capture continuously evolving external effects. To address this limitation, we introduce CTIA-ODE, a continuous-time forecasting framework centered on Continuous-Time Inter-Variable Attention (CTIA). Specifically, CTIA is embedded within an ordinary differential equation (ODE) solver, enabling the continuously evolving endogenous trajectory to dynamically query a static exogenous context along the integration path without requiring explicit temporal alignment. To improve the stability of the continuous latent dynamics, we further introduce a dual-stabilization strategy: architecturally, a Linear Residual Augmentation (LRA) module provides a macroscopic trend anchor, while an Outlier-Robust Hybrid Loss (ORHL) mitigates the influence of heavy-tailed anomalies during optimization. Extensive experiments across eight real-world datasets demonstrate that CTIA-ODE achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance across diverse datasets and prediction horizons, while maintaining a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off with a compact memory footprint and low inference latency, particularly under long-horizon forecasting settings. Anonymous code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CTIA-ODE-15A6/.

items.title: Rent-Seeking Language Models: Reward Models Set the Prices, Frequent Audits Curb the Rent
items.description: arXiv:2610.19832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reward model overoptimization in RLHF is usually described as reward hacking. We recast it as rent-seeking: the policy, a firm, earns reward from a regulator, the proxy reward model, that true quality does not back. The lens turns overoptimization into measurable quantities, namely rent, a capture index and deadweight loss, and into testable predictions from the economics of regulation. In a fixed, version-controlled testbed with three model families, accuracy-matched proxy reward models and two gold reward models, RL turns 41% to 66% of its proxy gain into rent while gold reward plateaus. Rent follows each regulator's prices. Neither proxy verifies facts, but one pays for confident specifics and the other for displays of diligence, so RL policies learn to fabricate details about nonexistent entities (97% to 100% of probes) or to deflect factual questions (67% to 98%). Kinship between policy and regulator adds a fixed premium of about 0.1 standard deviations but gives the policy no extra leverage under optimization. At a fixed expected fine, frequent mild audits beat rare severe ones, and random audits are as efficient per audit as targeted ones. Bringing the bunching estimator of tax economics to RL training, we also find a first sign that policies learn to stay just below a targeted audit's threshold.

items.title: Memory-Efficient Subspace Optimization with Residual Correction: From Momentum SGD to Muon
items.description: arXiv:2610.19844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory-efficient subspace optimization has emerged as a practical approach to reducing the memory cost of LLM training while preserving optimization performance. Previous algorithms typically rely on the leading singular subspace of stochastic gradients, yet the gradient noise may dominate the subspace in later training stages and can prevent convergence. To overcome this limitation, we adopt a residual correction framework, which maintains the optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to the parameter update. We first integrate this scheme into momentum SGD to develop SMRC, which attains an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for a fixed orthonormal basis, matching that of full-space momentum SGD. Our analysis introduces a subspace virtual iterate to resolve the coupling between the momentum and the residual correction. Furthermore, we extend SMRC to a multi-stage variant which periodically recomputes bases to track the evolving dominant subspace and retains the same rate. Since each basis refresh breaks the consistency of the virtual iterates, we devise a boundary correction approach that aligns them across stages. Beyond momentum SGD, we incorporate our framework into Muon and propose PMRC, which applies the matrix sign to the projected momentum. Through a weighted momentum tracking analysis that accounts for the residual gradient, we establish an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for PMRC, which matches the rate of full-space Muon. We also design a multi-stage PMRC with periodically refreshed bases, which maintains a convergence rate of the same order. Extensive experimental results confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithms.

items.title: Energy Consumption Analysis of Discrete Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.19855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to scale, their energy consumption during inference has become a critical concern. While Autoregressive (AR) models are the industry standard, Diffusion Language Models (DLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative capable of parallel token generation. In this paper, we perform a comparative energy benchmark of diffusion models (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B) against AR counterparts (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B). We analyze the trade-offs between model architecture, KV-cache optimization, and Joules-per-token efficiency. Our results show that at longer sequences (200--600 tokens), diffusion models achieve 2.5--2.7 J/token, approximately 2$\times$ more efficient than AR models with KV-cache (5.3--5.7 J/token). KV-cache provides substantial benefits for AR models at longer sequences (50--70\% energy reduction).

items.title: SPARS: A Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection Framework for Continual Learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.19876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual learning aims to acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned knowledge. However, updating shared parameters when learning new tasks often overwrites existing knowledge, causing catastrophic forgetting. Memory replay methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting but rely on previous samples, raising privacy, memory, and scalability concerns. On the other hand, parameter isolation-based methods preserve learned knowledge but may limit knowledge transfer, whereas regularization promotes adaptability but remains susceptible to interference between old and new tasks. To maintain the stability-plasticity trade-off, this paper proposes Stability-Plasticity-Aware Region Selection (SPARS), a replay-free hybrid framework combining global parameter isolation with localized parameter regularization. SPARS estimates parameter importance using either the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) or a novel Confidence Score (CS) estimator that leverages logit sensitivity and achieves comparable performance to FIM without requiring labelled data. Based on parameter importance, SPARS partitions parameters into three importance-aware regions namely, winning, neighboring, and non-important parameter regions. Each region receives a different adaptation strategy: selective freezing, soft regularization, or unrestricted learning based on its role in the stability-plasticity trade-off. To mitigate classifier bias in class-incremental learning, we employ Quadratic Discriminant Analysis to improve performance on previously learned classes .Experiments on CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet demonstrate consistent improvement in average incremental accuracy over existing isolation- and regularization-based methods across task- and class-incremental learning. On TinyImageNet, SPARS achieves the best performance with 6% improvement for class-incremental learning while retaining over 60% of parameters for future tasks.

items.title: Neural Wasserstein Splines: Representation-Invariant Second-Order Priors for Trajectory Inference
items.description: arXiv:2610.19878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Population dynamics are often observed only as unpaired snapshots, which leave the evolution between measurements underdetermined. Second-order regularization can constrain it, but a penalty on the accelerations of sampled particles is a prior on joint particle paths, and different particle representations of the same marginal curve can have different acceleration costs. We therefore introduce Neural Wasserstein Splines (NWSP), a sample-based method that learns a continuous population curve under a Wasserstein smoothness prior. A neural network maps latent variables to the control points of a cubic spline in time, so samples at any time come from the spline basis without numerical integration. We project the generator's velocity onto gradients of a finite dictionary of scalar potentials and differentiate this measure-dependent projection in time, obtaining a finite-dimensional surrogate for the intrinsic Wasserstein acceleration, trained jointly with distributional fit losses. For a fixed dictionary and ridge parameter, we prove that the population penalty depends only on the marginal curve and bound its sensitivity to moment-estimation errors. Learned potentials (NWSP-N) sharpen acceleration estimates. On various synthetic and single-cell benchmarks, NWSP is highly competitive with transport and flow-based methods, ranking in the top two in 11 of 16 settings. The penalty improves on an unregularized spline in 13 of 16 settings and, while competitive with a particle-acceleration penalty, adds provable representation invariance.

items.title: Occupancy Modeling via Drifting: One-Step Generation Enables Direct Policy Extraction
items.description: arXiv:2610.19883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing interest in behavior foundation models, combined with recent advancements in generative modeling, has led to an appealing recipe for reinforcement learning from unlabeled data: pre-train a generative model to model occupancies, i.e., discounted state visitations, on reward-free trajectories, such that a policy can be easily extracted once a small reward-labeled dataset becomes available. We decompose this recipe along three axes: (i) the degree to which the multi-modal structure of occupancies must be captured, (ii) the class of generative model, and (iii) the method used for policy extraction. Along each axis, we consider existing choices, propose simpler alternatives, and validate each decision experimentally. This analysis culminates in a novel, streamlined method that leverages drifting, a modern one-step generative sampler, to model the occupancy. We show that this enables policy extraction via direct differentiation through the occupancy model, and bypasses the need for critic distillation. Overall, we observe that this nimble setup leads to improvements in performance on standard benchmarks.

items.title: On the Limits of Representation-Based Test-Time Adaptation for Multimodal LLMs
items.description: arXiv:2610.19892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models suffer significant accuracy drops under common corruptions. While test-time adaptation (TTA) successfully mitigates these shifts in CLIP-like contrastive models, its application to generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains underexplored and uniquely challenging due to their sequential token generation. In this work, we demonstrate that representation-based TTA fails to recover performance in MLLMs. Our experiments reveal that even when violating standard TTA assumptions by leveraging target data offline, sample-blind feature alignment recovers only marginal accuracy. We attribute this failure to the nature of corruption shifts: unlike CLIP-like architectures, which benefit from a shared domain-shift direction within a single pooled classification embedding, MLLM visual token sequence shifts are nearly orthogonal and span the full embedding space.These findings bound what any sample-blind, position-shared correction at a single encoder site can achieve, establishing that representation-space interventions alone might be insufficient to ensure corruption robustness in MLLMs.

items.title: Universal Sample-Based Embeddings of Higher-Order Objects
items.description: arXiv:2610.19899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural networks operate naturally on finite-dimensional vectors, yet many problems require reasoning about higher-order objects such as distributions, functions, and graphs. Such objects capture relationships within a ground set and rarely admit an explicit compact representation. Moreover, we typically want a compact representation not of a single higher-order object but of an entire family of such objects, including members unseen during training. While a few approaches exist for particular object types, none is designed to work across object types. We propose a unified framework that represents any higher-order object as a fixed-size embedding vector learned over a family of such objects. An encoder maps an object, seen only through a finite set of samples, to an embedding, and a domain-specific decoder supplies the training signal by modeling the object conditioned on that embedding. Since the encoder works only from samples, one architecture serves different object types. Because the decoder is a model already suited to single instances of the object type, the framework inherits that model's native operations and inductive biases. We instantiate the framework on distributions, functions, and graphs. In each case we show that a single trained model represents an entire family and generalizes to members unseen during training. Furthermore, we demonstrate the downstream utility of these embeddings: interpolating distributions in embedding space, solving differential equations in embedding space, and predicting unseen edges from a graph's embedding.

items.title: When Non-Adversarial Noise Hurts Learning: Benchmarking Skill Self-Evolution in Agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.19910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly improve by distilling experience into reusable skills, but errors in that experience can persist in learned rules and affect later tasks. Existing evaluations largely examine clean learning or perturbations encountered after skills are frozen, leaving robustness during self-evolution insufficiently understood. We introduce RSE-Bench, to our knowledge the first benchmark for evaluating skill self-evolution under ordinary, non-adversarial noise. It spans four domains and six benchmarks, with controlled perturbations to instructions, environmental evidence, execution records, and outcome--record pairings that preserve the underlying tasks and native scoring rules. The protocol separates noise during learning from input-side noise at evaluation, testing frozen skill stores on held-out tasks. We also introduce \textsc{RSEClaw}, a method-agnostic framework supporting consistent noise injection and process diagnostics of actual exposure and skill updates. Across three methods and two backbones, noisy learning retains only $25.5\%$--$42.1\%$ of the aggregate gain achieved by clean self-evolution, depending on the noise type. Perturbations confined to execution records and outcome--record pairings cause average losses comparable to input-side noise, despite leaving the original executions and evaluations intact. Diagnostics further identify differences in candidate skill text that coexist with small changes in mean held-out performance.

items.title: CARD: Closing the Teacher-Student Loop for Adversarial Robustness Distillation
items.description: arXiv:2610.19911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adversarial robustness distillation typically treats a robust teacher as a fixed knowledge source and transfers robustness to a compact student in a one-way manner. This paradigm terminates teacher-student interaction once the student is distilled, thereby discarding potentially useful feedback from the distilled student. However, exploiting such feedback is nontrivial because indiscriminate weak-to-strong transfer may propagate student errors to the teacher. To address this issue, we propose Cyclic Adversarial Robustness Distillation (CARD), a closed-loop framework that turns the distilled student into a feedback source for refining the robust teacher and subsequently transfers the teacher gains back to the same student. CARD first performs strong-to-weak adversarial distillation and then uses reliability-enhanced student feedback to refine the robust teacher. The refinement combines inverse adversarial student feedback with teacher-student discrepancy maximization, after which the refined teacher is used to continue training the same student under the unchanged base distillation objective. We further establish a sample-level sufficient condition for reliable weak-to-strong feedback transfer and derive a distribution-level upper bound on the refined teacher's risk. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet-10 across multiple teacher-student architectures and base distillation methods show that CARD improves adversarial robustness in most evaluated settings while generally preserving clean accuracy. These results show that the distilled student can provide useful feedback to the teacher, enabling robustness transfer to proceed beyond the conventional one-way teacher-to-student paradigm.

items.title: Beyond DFT electronic band structures via dual-space orbital learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.19919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate electronic band structures are essential for predicting material properties, but high-fidelity calculations are computationally demanding. We introduce O-kRystal, a dual-space orbital-learning framework that uses a lower-cost Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) calculation as both an energy baseline and a source of structured orbital information. Combining PBE band energies with real- and reciprocal-space orbital matrices, O-kRystal predicts higher-level corrections for individual electronic states as a function of crystal momentum and spin. For states within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint, it predicts Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) band energies with a mean absolute error of $0.171 \pm 0.009$ eV across nearly 6,000 three-dimensional materials spanning insulating, metallic, magnetic, and nonmagnetic systems. On a separate benchmark of six strongly correlated materials, it reduces the corresponding PBE band-energy MAE by 68.7% and resolves orbital-dependent changes in the relative placement of transition-metal d and ligand p states. Despite training only at high-symmetry points, it maintains comparable accuracy at unseen points along band paths and reconstructs HSE06 densities of states from dense Brillouin-zone predictions. Finally, training O-kRystal on $G_0W_0$ quasiparticle energies for two-dimensional materials demonstrates its applicability across levels of theory and the potential of orbital learning for higher-fidelity, momentum-resolved electronic-structure prediction beyond density functional theory.

items.title: MorphingNet: Symbolic Regression Where the Network Is the Formula
items.description: arXiv:2610.19942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce MorphingNet, a network for symbolic regression (SR) whose units change their function continuously. Instead of searching over expressions built from a fixed operator library, MorphingNet trains the form of each function as a parameter, so SR becomes one continuous optimization problem. Its units are either pole-free rational functions or complex exponential--logarithm functions, which move between exponentials, sinusoids, damped oscillations, power laws and logarithms as their parameters change. The network is a readable formula at every step of training, and no operator library is needed to train it; a structure-recovery step afterwards rewrites the trained formula into short elementary expressions. Training is dense linear algebra, so it is GPU-friendly and scales to large data. MorphingNet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on SRBench, recovers most generating formulas on synthetic benchmarks, and on large data is up to two orders of magnitude faster than the strongest search method. By turning the search for a formula into the training of a network, MorphingNet offers a new paradigm for SR and for scientific discovery from data.

items.title: Learning Graph Energies for Finite-Time Generation
items.description: arXiv:2610.19946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energy-based models can represent distributions over discrete structures such as molecular graphs, but an energy that is accurate at equilibrium need not yield accurate samples when the sampler stops after a fixed number of steps. We introduce finite-horizon energy learning, which adapts the acceptance energy of a Metropolis--Hastings sampler to the distribution it returns after a prescribed number of steps, with initialization, proposals, and annealing schedule held fixed. For graph generation, a frozen pretrained model supplies initialization and proposals, and a learned energy governs acceptance. A training-only discriminator scores completed samples, and coupled continuations of the accepted and rejected branches of a proposal give an acceptance-gradient estimator that is unbiased for a fixed discriminator under stated conditions, without equilibrated negative samples or differentiation through discrete states. Generation uses the learned energy in the original single-trajectory sampler, without discriminator evaluations or reranking. On twelve pairwise binary targets with exactly evaluated terminal laws, learned energies have lower median terminal total variation than the equilibrium-correct energy in every tested short-horizon setting, and than its numerically tuned scalar multiple in most settings. On MOSES, a learned two-coefficient combination of pretrained Graph Energy Matching (GEM) potentials lowers FCD by 3.7--10.5\% relative to scale-calibrated GEM at matched sampling steps, with validity gains at the shortest budget and a sub-point validity trade-off at higher budgets.

items.title: Safe-FCL: Continual Risk Awareness and Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation for Federated Continual Learning of LLMs
items.description: arXiv:2610.19968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables large language models (LLMs) to learn collaboratively from distributed client data, but malicious client updates can compromise global model safety. As federated tasks evolve, changing malicious update patterns challenge the ability of existing defenses to maintain reliable risk detection over time. To address this challenge, we propose Safe-FCL, a framework integrating continual risk awareness with fine-grained safety aggregation for federated continual learning of LLMs. Specifically, the Continual Risk Awareness (CRA) mechanism learns emerging risk patterns across sequential tasks and constrains detector updates using a protective subspace derived from historical features, mitigating forgetting of previously learned malicious patterns while adapting to new risks. To translate risk awareness into aggregation-level safety control, the Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation (FGSA) mechanism combines client-level risk assessments from CRA with module-level deviations from historical update behavior to adaptively regulate aggregation contributions, suppressing potentially malicious updates while minimizing unnecessary restrictions on benign updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Safe-FCL outperforms current SOTA methods, improving global-model Rule and MD-Judge scores in federated continual learning by 0.41% and 0.64%, respectively, while increasing average risk recognition accuracy by 2.01%.

items.title: LatentLoop: Scaling Looped MoE Models with Asymmetric Compute Allocation
items.description: arXiv:2610.19975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine parameter reuse with sparse computation to improve performance under matched budgets. Prior work demonstrates that different loop visits can play different roles even when they share parameters. To probe the contributions of different loop visits, we learn separate residual coefficients in a model that applies a shared block twice, observing a smaller scale in the first visit. Fixed coefficient experiments show that reducing the first visit's scale preserves or improves performance, whereas the same reductions to the second hurt it. This asymmetry motivates us to explore asymmetric compute allocation. We propose \textbf{LatentLoop}, which compresses the first visit's sequence, retains full resolution in the second, and reallocates saved computation to increase the hidden size. We further learn how strongly the first visit updates the full sequence, and share MoE weights across visits while using separate attention parameters to accommodate their different sequence resolutions. Across 15 configurations spanning 1.3B--7B parameters, with the largest budget exceeding $10^{21}$ FLOPs, LatentLoop consistently lowers validation NLL. At a fitted NLL of 1.988, predicted compute savings are 19.0\% and 7.9\% relative to vanilla MoE and the looped baseline. It also improves average scores on nine benchmarks at all sizes in 0-shot and 5-shot settings. These results suggest asymmetric compute allocation is a promising direction for looped MoE models.

items.title: Empirical Boundaries of Reservoir Computing for Few-Shot Sequence Pattern Tasks
items.description: arXiv:2610.19997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient sequence modeling remains a fundamental challenge in machine learning. Despite the success of Transformers, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have recently re-emerged as efficient alternatives. Particularly, Echo State Networks (ESNs) offer a compelling framework of randomized RNNs that have been extensively studied for time-series forecasting and dynamical systems. This paper presents an empirical analysis of distributional, architectural, and optimization variants of ESNs evaluated on few-shot sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) pattern tasks. These synthetic tasks utilize discrete symbol sequences, characterized by delays, inactive phases, and triggered markers to isolate and evaluate memory and pattern recognition capabilities. The minimality of these tasks is crucial to understand the strengths and limitations of machine learning models. Furthermore, when the input signal utilizes a one-hot encoding, ESN dynamics are governed strictly by their weight distributions, offering an ideal lens through which to study reservoir computing. Our findings map the performance boundaries of ESNs relative to state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. We show that preserving a linear state regime is vital for memory tasks, such as pattern completion or simple copy. We propose a data-dependent modulation mechanism for nonlinear input injection into the reservoir (G-ESN). G-ESN functions as a statistical filter capable of solving tasks that conventional ESNs cannot (the adding problem and bracket matching). Finally, for Deep ESNs, we evaluate a shared readout mechanism across layers that outperforms conventional concatenated readouts on structural tasks, including selective copy, sorting problem, and bracket matching.

items.title: Provable Transformer Context Compression for In-Context Reinforcement Learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.20004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformers can perform in-context reinforcement learning without parameter updates. However, existing theoretical constructions often require context sizes that grow with the number of sampled transitions, leading to increasing memory costs in large-scale problems. This raises a fundamental scalability question: how much context is intrinsically necessary to carry out such learning? We answer this question for fixed-policy TD evaluation. We show that, with a shared linear decoder, the minimum context dimension required to exactly reproduce the first $L$ TD iterates is the Krylov dimension induced by the sampled transitions. When the available context dimension $m$ falls below this threshold, exact reproduction is no longer possible. In this regime, we characterize the optimal approximation error and show that it decays as $\Theta(\gamma^m\max\{1,1/(m(1-\gamma))\})$ where $\gamma$ is the discounting factor. Moving from representation complexity to actual memory cost, we characterize the optimal retained memory for exact continuous representations as $\Theta(nk_L)$ and show experimentally that on a sampled task whose exact rank is full but whose numerical rank is small, a context accurate to $10^{-2}$ is $88.7\%$ smaller than the sparse sufficient statistics of TD. Finally, we establish the learnability of the shared executor through pretraining by proving global convergence of an auxiliary objective over effective attention parameters under suitable task diversity. Experiments across diverse TD evaluation problems validate parameter recovery and the predicted context--accuracy tradeoff.

items.title: Outperforming 1000 Euclidean Layers With Hyperbolic Goal-Conditioned RL
items.description: arXiv:2610.20009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling self-supervised contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) to 1000-layer Euclidean neural networks has enabled state-of-the-art goal-reaching performance, yet wall-clock time scales linearly with depth. We find that changing the geometry achieves stronger performance with far shallower networks. This matters in complex navigation environments, where walls can make route distance deviate substantially from Euclidean distance. In a U-shaped maze, we show that the longer the route, the more it deviates from Euclidean distance. Hyperbolic CRL addresses this mismatch by replacing Euclidean distances in CRL's contrastive objective with geodesic distances in hyperbolic space. On hard navigation tasks, inductive bias beats scale: depth 64 hyperbolic agents outperform 1024-layer-deep Euclidean networks while training more than $12 \times$ faster and using about $13 \times$ fewer parameters. We observe that hyperbolic agents behave qualitatively better in hard humanoid mazes, where they follow corridors to reach goals, whereas Euclidean agents try straight-line shortcuts over walls. Our results show that matching the representation geometry to the task can substitute for substantial network depth. Code is at https://github.com/Probabilistic-and-Interactive-ML/HypGCRL .

items.title: ChemArgus: Automated Scientific Diagnostics for Lab-Grade Multimodal Chemistry Reasoning: A Frontier Benchmark
items.description: arXiv:2610.20012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chemistry evaluation has moved past multiple-choice probes toward open-ended expert problems, yet the benchmarks that define the current frontier still score answer endpoints alone. Such scoring conflates memorized facts with stepwise derivation, treats visual and textual inputs as interchangeable, and confounds long-horizon planning with stepwise execution. These blind spots prevent any diagnosis of where the reasoning chain breaks in a model. We present ChemArgus, a competition-level chemistry benchmark drawn from chemistry competition material, textbooks, and research papers, whose scoring replaces the answer endpoint with three measurement properties. Fine-grained scoring grades every subquestion point by point with partial credit, so a score lands at the level of the step rather than the outcome. Multimodal capability is priced on every problem containing a real image, paired with a controlled text description, so visual understanding is measured against text on identical tasks. Diagnostic attribution reads paired metrics that share one scoring unit and differ only in context construction, so a gap between two scores isolates a single cause, namely integration, propagation, or local reasoning. GPT-5.6-Sol scores 23.2% on unassisted whole-problem solving against 28.8% and 30.4% under the two sequential metrics, a gap measuring the integration burden. Through rubric partial credit and these cause-isolating score gaps, ChemArgus shows not only whether a model answers chemistry correctly but where its reasoning chain fails, so that every score it reports doubles as a diagnosis, a readout of the chain rather than a verdict, aiming to guide language models step by step on their path toward chemistry expertise, one corrected step at a time, each step priced by the rubric, point by point.

items.title: On the Convergence of Semi-Gradient TD: A Mean Field Perspective
items.description: arXiv:2610.20014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semi-gradient temporal-difference learning is a core algorithmic component of reinforcement learning, but bootstrapping with function approximation generally induces a non-conservative vector field and can lead to instability. We analyze this effect for two-layer neural networks in the mean-field regime and identify a simple stability mechanism in which entropy-induced relaxation dominates the sensitivity of the moving bootstrap target. Under this condition, we prove exponential convergence to a unique fixed point and quantify its bias relative to the unregularized Bellman solution. We also show that the same mechanism extends to entropy-regularized off-policy control through soft Q-learning.

items.title: Sequential Learning-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network Modeling for Parameter Estimation on a Power Converter
items.description: arXiv:2610.20041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A staged physics-informed neural network (PINN) is proposed for identifying the inductance, capacitance and parasitic resistances of a DC buck converter from time-domain data. Gradients are released in the order of L to C to rL to rC, a sequence derived from sensitivity analysis. The five-stage schedule recovers L and C to within 5% and the series ESR to 10%, while a three-stage variant attains the same accuracy 11% faster. An 84 factorial sweep confirms that the trained PINN remains accurate for simultaneous 8% perturbations of all four components, achieving a waveform RMSE of 2.6 x 10-2 over 5 ms-an order-of-magnitude better than a simultaneous-training baseline.

items.title: GBTSVR: Twin Support Vector Regression via Granular Ball Computing
items.description: arXiv:2610.20053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Regression models used in real-world applications are often challenged by noise, outliers, data heterogeneity, and asymmetric error characteristics, which severely limit the effectiveness of conventional point-wise learning models. While twin support vector regression (TSVR) partially addresses these issues through the use of nonparallel regression bounds, it still relies on individual samples as basic learning units. As a result, TSVR remains highly sensitive to noisy and contaminated observations and fails to leverage the underlying structural and regional information inherent in complex datasets, leading to suboptimal robustness and generalization performance. To address these limitations, we introduce granular ball twin support vector regression (GBTSVR) and its quantile extension, granular ball twin support vector quantile regression (GB-TSVQR). The proposed models integrate granular ball computing with TSVR, replacing individual data points with compact, structure-preserving granular balls as fundamental learning units. This region-level representation effectively suppresses noise and outliers while preserving intrinsic data geometry, thereby enhancing robustness, stability, and generalization. GBTSVR constructs nonparallel lower- and upper-bound regression functions over granular balls, significantly reducing sensitivity to sample-level perturbations. Building upon this framework, GB-TSVQR further incorporates quantile regression principles to simultaneously capture heterogeneous trends and asymmetric error distributions across different quantile levels. Extensive experiments on synthetic datasets, time-series benchmarks, and outlier-contaminated data demonstrate that the proposed GBTSVR and GB-TSVQR consistently outperform state-of-the-art regression models.

items.title: Trainable at Depth, Solvable at Small Size: What the Loss Surface of a Polynomial Activation Dictates for Designing, Initializing and Training Networks
items.description: arXiv:2610.20069v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What makes a deep network train, and what shape is its loss surface? We answer both with one construction at two scales: a polynomial activation f (z) = z + {\lambda}z 3 , clamped and projected onto the unit sphere, plus an unnormalized identity path. As a deep stack it trains to one hundred layers on MNIST with no normalization machinery; as a small model its square loss is a polynomial system we solve exactly. The small scale explains the large one: it prescribes how to design, initialize and train the stack.

items.title: Rethinking Prediction Horizons: Decoupling Model Queries from State Updates in Few-Step MeanFlow
items.description: arXiv:2610.20071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: MeanFlow predicts interval-average velocities, but conventional few-step sampling ties the interval queried from the model to the duration of the state update. We separate these two quantities at inference, fixing the model, update grid, and number of queries while varying the prediction horizon. Our central finding is that the horizon response depends on both query position and the states entering that query. Across seven independently trained CIFAR-10 checkpoints at classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale 2, a longer horizon worsens FID at early steps but improves it at the midpoint. To probe whether query time alone determines this response, we fix the midpoint query and current/subsequent guidance while changing only earlier CFG.
